Chapter 1 — Introduction: how is it examined?
column4:
2 hrs  \(\cdot\) asked in all 23 papers  \(\cdot\) 3 syllabus sub-topics  \(\cdot\) no numerical component.
Read this first:
  • Shortest chapter in the syllabus, but every single paper opens with it, usually as Q1 for 4 to 6 marks. Cheapest marks in the subject.
  • Only two questions are ever asked, in rotation:
    • Narrate the evolution (1G \(\rightarrow\) 5G) TOP 10,
    • Compare the generations in terms of technology advancement TOP 9.
  • Both are answered from one table (§1.3). Learn that table and the chapter is finished.
  • Two small riders recur: forward and reverse channel HOT 4 and trends beyond 3G / 5G HOT 4. 2 marks each, one line each.
  • Do not write history as prose. The examiner wants generation, access technique, modulation, data rate, example system. Dates alone score badly.

column1: Briefly explain the evolution of wireless / mobile communications
column4:
Milestones, before cellular
  • 1877: first wire-line telephone in commercial use.
  • 1897: Marconi demonstrates radio to a tug 18 miles at sea.
  • Until 1934: mobile radio \(=\) AM, used only by police and public bodies.
  • 1935: Armstrong invents FM \(\rightarrow\) becomes the mobile standard for the next 40 years.
  • 1946: first public mobile telephone service, 25 US cities.
    • Single high-power transmitter, tall tower, range over 50 km.
    • Half-duplex push-to-talk, 120 kHz of RF for 3 kHz of speech.
  • 1950: US regulator doubles the channels, no new spectrum. Bandwidth per channel halved to 60 kHz, later 30 kHz.
  • Late 1950s / 60s: IMTS (Improved Mobile Telephone Service) adds full duplex, auto-dial, auto-trunking.
Milestones, cellular era
  • 1960s: AT&T Bell Labs develop cellular radiotelephony theory.
  • 1968: AT&T proposes a cellular system to the US regulator.
  • 1979: NTT, Japan. World's first commercial cellular system.
  • 1983: AMPS starts in the USA. The regulator allocates 40 MHz in the 800 MHz band \(=\) 666 duplex channels of 30 kHz each way.
  • 1990 onwards: 2G digital systems, GSM and DCS 1800.
  • 1995: 3G standardisation starts, IMT-2000 / UMTS.
  • 2000s: 3G deployed, then 4G LTE.
  • 2020: 5G commercial.
The bottleneck that forced the cellular idea
  • Bell Mobile Phone, New York, 1976:
    • market of 10,000,000 people, 12 channels, 543 paying customers, waiting list over 3,700.
  • Spectrum is fixed by the regulator \(\rightarrow\) capacity could not grow by adding transmitters.
  • Only fix left: reuse the same frequencies inside the same city. That is the cellular concept (Ch 2).
Worldwide market penetration +Fig
  • Mobile telephony was introduced in 1946 but sat below 0.1 % penetration for 35 years, until cellular arrived.
  • Once cellular started it grew faster than any earlier consumer technology: US cellular users 25,000 (1984) \(\rightarrow\) 16 million (1994), growth over 50 % per year.
  • This is the point of the figure: the curve is flat while the technology is pre-cellular, then turns almost vertical.
Growth of mobile telephony against other consumer technologies. Note the 35-year flat start. Rappaport Fig 1.1
Answer skeleton 4 6
  1. Pre-cellular era (1946–1979): one high-power transmitter, no reuse, a dozen channels per city \(\rightarrow\) blocked calls, waiting lists.
  2. Cellular idea (1968–1979): many low-power cells \(+\) frequency reuse \(\rightarrow\) capacity grows w/o new spectrum.
  3. 1G (1983): analog, FDMA/FDD, AMPS.
  4. 2G (1990s): digital, TDMA or CDMA, GSM / IS-95.
  5. 2.5G: packet data bolted on, GPRS / EDGE.
  6. 3G (2000s): IP + broadband, W-CDMA / cdma2000.
  7. 4G (2010s): all-IP, OFDMA + MIMO, LTE.
  8. 5G (2020): mmWave, massive MIMO, IoT.
For a 6-mark answer add one line of why each step happened. The examiner is looking for the driver, not just the date.

column1: Define forward and reverse channel
column4:
Three transmission modes
  • Simplex: one direction only. Eg paging, broadcast radio.
  • Half duplex: both directions, not at once. One radio channel, push-to-talk. Eg walkie-talkie.
  • Full duplex: both directions simultaneously. Needs two channels, or one channel split in time.
Duplexing \(=\) how full duplex is achieved
  • FDD, frequency division duplexing:
    • Two separate frequencies, one per direction.
    • Separated by a frequency gap (guard band) so the handset's own transmitter does not swamp its receiver.
    • Eg AMPS and GSM: forward and reverse bands 45 MHz apart.
    • Needs a duplexer (costly RF filter) in every handset.
  • TDD, time division duplexing:
    • One frequency, shared in time. Part of each frame carries BS \(\rightarrow\) MS, the rest MS \(\rightarrow\) BS.
    • No duplexer needed \(\rightarrow\) cheaper, smaller handset.
    • Only possible with digital transmission, and only over short ranges, because propagation delay eats the guard time.
    • Sensitive to timing. Eg DECT cordless, WiMAX, 5G NR.
FDD: two frequencies, permanent guard gap.
TDD: one frequency, direction toggled in time.
Forward and reverse channel (the 2-mark definition)
  • Forward channel \(=\) downlink \(=\) base station \(\rightarrow\) mobile.
  • Reverse channel \(=\) uplink \(=\) mobile \(\rightarrow\) base station.
  • The air interface defines four physical channels, not two:
    • forward voice / data channel (FVC), reverse voice / data channel (RVC),
    • forward control channel (FCC), reverse control channel (RCC).
  • Control channels carry setup, paging and service requests. About 5 % of the total channels.
  • Reverse link is the harder one to design: the handset has a small battery and a poor antenna, so the reverse link limits cell radius (see the Ch 3 link budget numericals).
A basic cellular system. Every BS reaches the MSC, and the MSC reaches the PSTN.

The two upgrade paths. Top: GSM \(\rightarrow\) GPRS \(\rightarrow\) EDGE \(\rightarrow\) W-CDMA \(\rightarrow\) HSPA \(\rightarrow\) LTE. Bottom: IS-95A \(\rightarrow\) IS-95B \(\rightarrow\) cdma2000 1x \(\rightarrow\) EV-DO \(\rightarrow\) LTE. Both converge on LTE, which is why LTE won.
2.5G protocols, with their rates
  • HSCSD (TDMA path): 57.6 kbps. Still circuit switched, just more timeslots.
  • GPRS (TDMA path): 171.2 kbps. First packet-switched service.
  • EDGE (TDMA path): 384 kbps. Same slots, 8-PSK instead of GMSK.
  • IS-95B (CDMA path): 64 kbps.
3G family, with their rates
  • W-CDMA / UMTS: 2.048 Mbps. Evolution of GSM, IS-136 and PDC.
  • cdma2000 1xRTT: 307 kbps. Evolution of IS-95.
  • cdma2000 1xEV-DO: over 2.4 Mbps, data optimised.
  • cdma2000 1xEV-DV: 144 kbps, data \(+\) voice.
What actually changed: 1G to 3G (write this, not the dates)
  • 1G \(\rightarrow\) 2G: analog \(\rightarrow\) digital.
    • Digital speech coding \(\rightarrow\) more users in the same band.
    • Error control coding \(\rightarrow\) works at lower SIR \(\rightarrow\) smaller \(N\).
    • Encryption and authentication become possible. 1G had neither.
    • SMS and low-rate data appear.
  • 2G \(\rightarrow\) 2.5G: circuit \(\rightarrow\) packet.
    • 2G was designed before the web \(\rightarrow\) data only over a modem, 9.6 kbps.
    • GPRS adds a packet core, user pays per byte not per minute.
    • No new radio spectrum is needed, only new protocols \(\rightarrow\) cheap upgrade.
  • 2.5G \(\rightarrow\) 3G: narrowband \(\rightarrow\) wideband.
    • 5 MHz W-CDMA carrier instead of 200 kHz \(\rightarrow\) Mbps rates.
    • Simultaneous voice \(+\) data, video calling, multimedia.
    • Soft handoff and RAKE reception become standard (Ch 5).
What actually changed: 3G to 5G
  • 3G \(\rightarrow\) 4G: all-IP and OFDM.
    • Circuit-switched core removed entirely, voice carried over IP.
    • OFDMA \(\rightarrow\) immune to frequency-selective fading w/o a complex equalizer (Ch 4, Ch 5).
    • MIMO \(\rightarrow\) spatial multiplexing \(\rightarrow\) capacity rises w/o more spectrum.
    • Scalable bandwidth 1.4 to 20 MHz, and much lower latency.
  • 4G \(\rightarrow\) 5G: one service \(\rightarrow\) three.
    • eMBB (fast broadband), URLLC (1 ms latency), mMTC (a million devices per km\(^2\)).
    • mmWave spectrum, massive MIMO, beamforming, network slicing.

column1: Discuss the basic trends in wireless communication beyond 3G, focusing on the key technological changes
column4:
The four enabling technologies of 4G
  • OFDM / OFDMA: splits a wideband channel into many narrow flat-fading sub-carriers \(\rightarrow\) removes the need for a complex time-domain equalizer (Ch 4).
  • MIMO: multiple antennas both ends \(\rightarrow\) parallel spatial streams \(\rightarrow\) capacity multiplies w/o extra spectrum.
  • Adaptive modulation and coding: the modulation order follows the instantaneous SNR \(\rightarrow\) near-Shannon efficiency.
  • All-IP flat architecture: no circuit core, fewer nodes \(\rightarrow\) lower latency, cheaper backhaul.
5G: what is genuinely new verified/added
  • Millimetre wave (24 to 100 GHz): huge bandwidth available.
    • Cost: severe path loss and blockage \(\rightarrow\) forces very small cells.
  • Massive MIMO: 64 to 256 antenna elements at the BS.
    • Narrow beams steered per user \(\rightarrow\) interference falls, range recovers.
  • NOMA, non-orthogonal multiple access: several users share one resource block at different power levels, separated by successive interference cancellation (Ch 7).
  • D2D, device-to-device: handsets talk directly, bypassing the BS.
  • Dense heterogeneous networks: macro, micro, pico and femto cells overlaid (Ch 2).
  • C-RAN, cloud radio access network: baseband processing centralised, only the radio head stays at the mast.
  • Network slicing: one physical network, several virtual networks with different latency and reliability guarantees.
  • IoT / mMTC: up to \(10^6\) low-power devices per km\(^2\).
Other 4G features worth listing
  • Interactive multimedia, streaming video, VoIP.
  • Global roaming and service portability.
  • High capacity at low cost per bit.
  • Ad hoc and multi-hop relaying.
  • Better spectral efficiency (bps/Hz) than any earlier generation.
The 3 service classes (the cleanest way to say 5G Vs 4G)
  • eMBB: enhanced mobile broadband, 1 to 20 Gbps.
  • URLLC: ultra-reliable low latency, 1 ms, for vehicles and industry.
  • mMTC: massive machine type communication, for IoT.
  • 4G offered one pipe. 5G offers three, tuned differently.

Cordless Vs cellular (the contrast that is examinable)
  • Cordless
    • Low mobility, low range, low speed.
    • Low power \(\rightarrow\) long battery life, cheap handset.
    • No handoff between base units, and no roaming.
    • High circuit quality, because the link is short.
  • Cellular
    • High mobility, wide area, vehicular speed.
    • Handoff and roaming supported \(\rightarrow\) complex switching (MSC).
    • Higher transmit power (\(\sim\)2 W at the handset) \(\rightarrow\) heavier battery.
    • Integrated with the PSTN.
Personal wireless communication (PCS / PCN)
  • PCS \(=\) personal communication services: the service concept, one personal number reaching a user anywhere.
  • PCN \(=\) personal communication network: the network that delivers PCS.
  • In the US, “PCS” also names the 1900 MHz band auctioned in 1994.
  • Design aim: pocket handset, low power, small cells, indoor + outdoor coverage.
  • PCS is a marketing / regulatory term, not a radio technology. Say that, then describe whichever air interface the question names.
Where the spectrum sits verified/added
  • VLF / LF: submarine, ground wave.
  • MF / HF: AM, short wave, ionospheric reflection.
  • VHF / UHF: FM radio, TV, all cellular. Small antennas, reliable mobile links.
  • SHF: microwave links 2 to 40 GHz, satellite C / Ku / Ka bands.
  • EHF: mmWave, 5G.
  • All of it is licensed and regulated to prevent interference (Ch 8).

column4:
4 hrs  \(\cdot\) asked in 21 of 23 papers  \(\cdot\) 5 syllabus sub-topics  \(\cdot\) heavy numerical load \(\rightarrow\) see the Ch 2 numerical companion.
Read this first:
  • Two questions carry the chapter. Handoff TOP 8 and the proof \(Q=\sqrt{3N}\) TOP 6. Bank both and most papers are already covered.
  • Everything in this chapter hangs off one trade-off: small \(N\) \(\rightarrow\) more capacity but worse SIR. Large \(N\) \(\rightarrow\) better SIR but less capacity. Say that sentence in any answer here and it will fit.
  • The examiner reliably pairs a theory part with a numerical part (prove \(Q=\sqrt{3N}\), then find optimal \(N\) for a given SIR). Do not learn the proof without the numerical.

column1: What is the cellular concept? What is a cell footprint? Explain interference tier
column4:
The problem it solved
  • Early mobile radio \(=\) one high-power transmitter on a tall tower.
    • Large coverage, but the same frequencies could never be reused inside it.
    • Bell's New York system supported 12 simultaneous calls over 1000 square miles.
  • Spectrum is fixed by the regulator \(\rightarrow\) capacity could not grow.
Advantages of going cellular
  • Low transmit power \(\rightarrow\) smaller batteries, cheaper hardware, less interference.
  • Frequency reuse \(\rightarrow\) capacity grows w/o new spectrum.
  • Capacity can be grown later by splitting cells, w/o redesigning the system.
The cellular idea (3 system-level ideas)
  • Replace one high-power transmitter with many low-power transmitters, each covering a small area called a cell.
  • Give neighbouring cells different channel groups \(\rightarrow\) interference stays low.
  • Reuse the same channel set at cells far enough apart.
  • Result: high capacity in a fixed spectrum, with no new technology.
Why a hexagon +Fig
  • The ideal contour is a circle, but circles either overlap (double coverage) or leave gaps (no coverage).
  • Only 3 regular shapes tile a plane w/o gaps or overlap: triangle, square, hexagon.
  • For the same distance from centre to the farthest edge, the hexagon covers the largest area \(\rightarrow\) fewest cells, fewest base stations, lowest cost.
  • Hexagon is also the closest of the three to a circle \(\rightarrow\) best match to a real omni-directional antenna pattern.
  • It has exactly 6 equidistant neighbours, and centre-to-centre lines are separated by multiples of \(60^\circ\) \(\rightarrow\) makes the reuse geometry solvable.
Terms
  • Cell \(=\) area covered by one cellular transmitter. The transmitter site itself \(=\) cell site.
  • Cell footprint \(=\) the actual radio coverage of a cell.
    • Real footprints are irregular (terrain, buildings).
    • Irregular footprints are tolerable at first, but as cells are added they break the reuse plan and cause co-channel interference.
    • So a regular shape is assumed for planning.
  • Cluster \(=\) the \(N\) cells that together use the complete channel set.
  • Co-channel cells \(=\) cells using the same channel set as the target cell.
  • Interference tier \(=\) a set of co-channel cells all at the same distance from the reference cell.
    • The nearest such set \(=\) first tier.
    • In hexagonal geometry the first tier always has exactly 6 cells.
    • Second and higher tiers are much further away, so their interference is normally neglected.
First tier: 6 co-channel cells, all at distance \(D\) from the reference cell.

column1: Explain the frequency reuse concept and the co-channel reuse ratio
column4:
Frequency reuse / frequency planning
  • Each BS gets a group of channels, used only inside its own cell.
  • Neighbouring cells get different groups.
  • Because coverage is confined to the cell, the same group can be reused at a cell far enough away.
  • Design task \(=\) choose the reuse pattern so interference stays tolerable.
Capacity arithmetic (learn this, it is the base of every numerical)
  • \(S\) \(=\) total duplex channels in the system.
  • \(k\) \(=\) channels per cell.
  • \(N\) \(=\) cells per cluster (cluster size).
  • \(M\) \(=\) number of times the cluster is replicated.
  • So \(S = kN\), and system capacity \[ C \;=\; MkN \;=\; MS \]
  • Capacity is directly proportional to \(M\), the number of replications.
  • Frequency reuse factor \(= 1/N\): each cell gets \(1/N\) of the total channels.
  • Typical \(N = 4, 7, 12\).
  • Small \(N\) \(\rightarrow\) cluster repeats more often \(\rightarrow\) higher capacity, but co-channel cells sit closer \(\rightarrow\) worse interference.
Cells with the same letter use the same channel set.
Which \(N\) are allowed
  • Hexagons only tile for \[ N \;=\; i^2 + ij + j^2 \qquad i,j = 0,1,2,\dots \]
  • Allowed \(N\): 1, 3, 4, 7, 9, 12, 13, 16, 19, 21, …
  • Eg \(i=1,j=1 \rightarrow N=3\). \(i=2,j=1 \rightarrow N=7\). \(i=3,j=2 \rightarrow N=19\).
Locating the co-channel cells (use the figure above)
  • From the centre of any cell:
    • move \(i\) cells perpendicular to one of the 6 faces,
    • turn \(60^\circ\), move \(j\) cells.
  • That lands on a co-channel cell. Repeating for all 6 faces gives the whole first tier.
  • Clockwise and counter-clockwise turns give the two mirror routes.
Channel assignment strategies 4
Fixed channel assignment (FCA)
  • Each cell gets a predetermined set of voice channels.
  • A new call can only use an unused channel of that cell.
  • If all of the cell's channels are busy, the call is blocked, even when a neighbour is idle.
  • Simple, no signalling overhead, predictable.
  • Borrowing variation: a busy cell may borrow a channel from a neighbour, supervised by the MSC, provided it does not break the reuse plan.
Dynamic channel assignment (DCA)
  • Channels are not owned by any cell. They sit in a central pool at the MSC.
  • On each request the MSC allocates a channel after checking
    • the candidate channel is unused in that cell,
    • and no co-channel cell within the reuse distance is using it.
  • Lowers blocking probability, raises capacity because it follows the traffic.
  • Cost: the MSC must collect occupancy and signal-strength data continuously \(\rightarrow\) heavy storage and computation load.
\(i=4\), \(j=2\): the 6 nearest co-channel A cells.

column1: What is handoff? Explain the handover process and the types of handover with application
column4:
Definition
  • A mobile moves out of one cell into another while a call is in progress.
  • The MSC transfers the call to a new channel belonging to the new BS.
  • That transfer \(=\) handoff (US) \(=\) handover (Europe).
  • Must be transparent: the user should not notice it.
The handoff process, step by step
  • Serving BS continuously measures the received signal strength on each reverse voice channel \(\rightarrow\) tells the MSC roughly where each mobile is.
  • Signal drops below the handoff threshold \(P_{r,\text{handoff}}\).
  • MSC identifies a candidate BS whose signal is stronger.
  • MSC checks the candidate has a free channel.
  • MSC re-allocates voice and control channels to the new BS.
  • Call continues on the new channel, old channel returns to the pool.
Improper Vs proper handoff (76 Bh 4, 81 Ba 1+3). Top: the level is left to fall past the minimum usable value before handoff is attempted \(\rightarrow\) call terminated at B. Bottom: handoff is made while the signal is still usable \(\rightarrow\) call transferred to BS 2.
Handoff threshold and handoff margin (75 Bh asks for the margin +Fig, 3)
  • \(P_{r,\text{minimum usable}}\) \(=\) weakest signal that still gives acceptable voice, typically \(-90\) to \(-100\) dBm.
  • \(P_{r,\text{handoff}}\) \(=\) level at which handoff is started. Always set a little higher.
  • Handoff margin \[ \Delta \;=\; P_{r,\text{handoff}} - P_{r,\text{minimum usable}} \]
  • \(\Delta\) too large \(\rightarrow\) handoffs fire needlessly \(\rightarrow\) MSC is burdened.
  • \(\Delta\) too small \(\rightarrow\) not enough time to finish the handoff \(\rightarrow\) call drops.
  • 1G analog: \(\Delta \approx\) 6 to 12 dB, handoff takes about 10 s.
  • 2G (GSM): \(\Delta \approx\) 0 to 6 dB, handoff takes 1 to 2 s.
Types of handoff
  • Hard handoff \(=\) “break before make”.
    • Old connection is released before the new one is set up.
    • Used in FDMA and TDMA systems (AMPS, GSM), where the two cells are on different frequencies.
    • Risk: if the new channel fails, the call drops.
  • Soft handoff \(=\) “make before break”.
    • New connection is set up before the old one is released, so the mobile is briefly served by two BSs at once.
    • Only possible in CDMA, where every cell uses the same frequency.
    • Gives BS diversity at the cell boundary \(\rightarrow\) far fewer dropped calls.
  • Intra-cell handoff: same BS, different channel. Used to escape interference or a deep fade.
  • Inter-cell handoff: between two cells of the same MSC.
  • Intersystem handoff: mobile leaves the coverage of one MSC and enters a system run by a different MSC. Needs an inter-MSC link and a roaming agreement.
How the handoff decision is taken (handoff measurement)
  • 1G analog: the BS measures signal strength, the MSC decides. A spare receiver, the locator receiver, scans neighbouring cells' mobiles.
  • 2G TDMA: mobile assisted handoff (MAHO).
    • The mobile measures received power from surrounding BSs and reports continuously to its serving BS.
    • Handoff triggers when a neighbour becomes appreciably stronger.
    • Much faster (1 to 2 s) because the MSC no longer has to poll every BS.

    • A steep short-term average \(\rightarrow\) handoff must be made quickly.

column1: Explain two schemes for prioritizing handoff
column4:
• Why prioritize: a dropped call is judged far more serious by the subscriber than a blocked call. So handoff requests must beat new-call requests.
  • Scheme 1: guard channels.
    • A fixed fraction of each cell's channels is reserved exclusively for handoff requests.
    • Simple, immediate.
    • Cost: those channels sit idle for new calls \(\rightarrow\) total carried traffic falls.
    • Fixed by using dynamic channel assignment for the reserved pool.
  • Scheme 2: queuing of handoff requests.
    • A handoff request that finds no free channel is put in a queue instead of being refused.
    • Works because there is a finite window between the signal dropping below the handoff threshold and dropping below the minimum usable level.
    • That window leaves room to wait for a channel to free up.
    • Reduces the probability of forced termination, but does not eliminate it.

column1: Practical handoff considerations
column4:
• Users move at wildly different speeds.
    • High-speed vehicle users need frequent handoffs.
    • Pedestrians may need none at all in a whole call.
  • Microcells make it worse. Small cells raise capacity, but the MSC is swamped when fast users are handed between them every few seconds.
  • Umbrella cell is the standard fix +Fig.
    • A large, high, high-power cell is overlaid on a group of microcells at the same site.
    • High-speed traffic is put on the umbrella cell \(\rightarrow\) few handoffs.
    • Low-speed traffic is put on the microcells \(\rightarrow\) high capacity.
    • Speed is estimated from the rate of change of the short-term signal average.
Umbrella cell: one large cell for fast traffic sitting over the microcells that serve slow traffic.
  • Cell dragging (72 Ash, 73 Bh ask for this by name, 2).
    • A pedestrian with a clear LOS to the BS keeps a very strong signal.
    • The level never falls to the handoff threshold, so no handoff is triggered.
    • The user travels deep into a neighbouring cell while still held by the old BS.
    • Result: severe interference in the neighbouring cell, and the reuse plan is broken.
    • Fixed by tuning the handoff threshold and averaging window carefully.
  • Handoff requests outrank new calls so that GoS is preserved.
Handoff strategy used in GSM (70 Ma, 8)
  • GSM uses MAHO, so the mobile does the measuring.
  • In every idle timeslot the mobile measures the BCCH power of up to 16 neighbouring cells and reports the best 6 to its BS twice per second.
  • Decision uses RXLEV (level) and RXQUAL (bit error rate), not level alone.
  • So GSM will hand a call off for poor quality even when the level is high, which a level-only 1G system cannot do.
  • Handoff is hard (break before make) and completes in 1 to 2 s.
  • Four cases: intra-cell, inter-cell within one BSC, between two BSCs of one MSC, and between two MSCs.

column1: Explain co-channel interference and adjacent channel interference
column4:
Sources of interference
  • Another mobile in the same cell.
  • A call in progress in a neighbouring cell.
  • Other base stations operating in the same frequency band.
  • Any non-cellular system leaking energy into the cellular band.
  • Interference is the limiting factor on capacity, not noise.
  • On voice channels it causes cross-talk and audible noise.
  • On control channels it causes missed and blocked calls through signalling errors.
Co-channel interference (CCI)Adjacent channel interference (ACI)
CauseAnother cell using the same frequencySignal in a nearby frequency leaking through an imperfect receiver filter
Comes fromCo-channel cells, one reuse distance awayChannels next to the wanted one, often inside the same cell
Depends on\(Q = D/R\) and cluster size \(N\)Filter sharpness and the near–far geometry
Independent ofTransmit power (raising all powers raises S and I equally)
Cured byIncreasing \(D/R\), ie a larger \(N\). SectoringChannel allocation w/ maximum frequency separation. Sharp band-pass filters. Power control
Adjacent channel interference in detail
  • Receiver filters are not ideal \(\rightarrow\) energy from neighbouring frequencies leaks into the passband.
  • Near–far problem is the worst case +Fig.
    • A mobile close to the BS transmits on a channel adjacent to one used by a mobile far from the BS.
    • The near mobile's signal arrives far stronger.
    • The BS then cannot hear the far mobile at all.
  • Cures:
    • Channel allocation: never give a cell channels that are adjacent in frequency. Keep separation as large as possible.
    • Careful filtering: sharp band-pass filter at the receiver, plus modulation w/ low out-of-band radiation.
    • Separate multiplexing for uplink and downlink.
    • Power control (below).
Power control syllabus, no PYQ yet
  • Every mobile transmits the smallest power that still holds a good reverse link.
  • Benefits:
    • Solves the near–far problem: the near mobile is turned down until the far mobile is audible again.
    • Longer battery life.
    • Raises reverse-link SIR across the whole system.
  • Essential, not optional, in CDMA, where every user in every cell shares one radio channel, so one loud mobile can jam a whole cell.

column1: Prove that the co-channel reuse ratio \(Q=\sqrt{3N}\), and derive S/I
column4:
Step 1: what \(Q\) is
  • \(R\) \(=\) cell radius (centre to vertex).
  • \(D\) \(=\) distance to the centre of the nearest co-channel cell.
  • Co-channel reuse ratio \(Q = D/R\).
  • When all cells are about the same size, CCI is independent of transmit power and depends only on \(R\) and \(D\).
  • Larger \(Q\) \(\rightarrow\) less interference but less capacity. The whole design is this trade-off.
First tier for \(N=7\). Worst case: the mobile sits at the cell boundary (point A), so its wanted signal is at its minimum while the interferers are at their nearest. Exact distances are \(D-R\), \(D\), \(D\), \(D\), \(D\), \(D+R\), but the approximation \(D_i = D\) is used for easy analysis.
Step 2: hexagonal geometry
  • Put the cell centres on the axes \(u,v\) separated by \(60^\circ\).
  • Distance between two adjacent cell centres \(= \sqrt{3}\,R\).
  • Move \(i\) cells along \(u\), then \(j\) cells along \(v\) at \(60^\circ\).
  • By the cosine rule w/ the included angle \(=60^\circ\), \[ D^2 = \left(i\sqrt{3}R\right)^2 + \left(j\sqrt{3}R\right)^2 - 2\left(i\sqrt{3}R\right)\left(j\sqrt{3}R\right)\cos 120^\circ \] \[ D^2 = 3R^2\left(i^2+j^2+ij\right) \]
  • But \(N = i^2+ij+j^2\), so \(D^2 = 3NR^2\), giving \[ \boxed{\;D = \sqrt{3N}\,R \quad\Longrightarrow\quad Q = \frac{D}{R} = \sqrt{3N}\;} \]
Step 3: signal to interference ratio
  • Received power falls as \(P_r \propto d^{-n}\), path loss exponent \(n = 2\) to \(4\).
  • With \(N_I\) interfering cells, \[ \frac{S}{I} \;=\; \frac{S}{\sum_{i=1}^{N_I} I_i} \;=\; \frac{R^{-n}}{\sum_{i=1}^{N_I} D_i^{-n}} \]
  • Take the worst case: mobile at the cell edge, first tier only, \(N_I = 6\), all \(D_i = D\): \[ \frac{S}{I} \;=\; \frac{R^{-n}}{6\,D^{-n}} \;=\; \frac{(D/R)^n}{6} \;=\; \frac{Q^n}{6} \;=\; \frac{\left(\sqrt{3N}\right)^n}{6} \]
  • Inverting for design, \[ \boxed{\;Q = \sqrt{3N} = \left(6\cdot \frac{S}{I}\right)^{1/n} \;\Longrightarrow\; N = \frac{Q^2}{3}\;} \]
  • Then round \(N\) up to the next allowed \(i^2+ij+j^2\).
Exact worst case for \(N=7\), and what sectoring does to it
  • Keeping the true distances instead of \(D_i = D\), and \(n = 4\): \[ \frac{S}{I} = \frac{R^{-4}}{2(D-R)^{-4} + 2(D+R)^{-4} + 2D^{-4}} \]
  • For \(N=7\), \(Q = 4.6\):
    • approximate result \(\;\rightarrow\; 49.56 \;=\; 17\;\text{dB}\),
    • exact result \(\;\rightarrow\; 17.8\) dB.
  • Both fall just short of the 18 dB that AMPS demands.
  • Going to the next size, \(N = 12\) (\(i=j=2\)), fixes SIR but cuts spectrum utilisation from \(1/7\) to \(1/12\) \(\rightarrow\) not tolerable.
  • So the answer is sectoring, not a bigger \(N\).
  • With \(120^\circ\) sectoring and 7-cell reuse, a mobile is hit by only 2 of the 6 first-tier co-channel cells.
  • SIR rises from 17 dB to about 24.2 dB.
  • That margin is then spent on reducing \(N\), which raises capacity.
\(120^\circ\) sectoring: of the 6 first-tier co-channel cells, only 2 have antenna patterns radiating into the centre cell.

column1: Define grade of service. How is it measured in a blocked-calls-cleared trunking system?
column4:
What trunking is
  • A large user population shares a small pool of channels.
  • A channel is allocated per call and returned to the pool the moment the call ends.
  • Works because users do not all call at once: it exploits their statistical behaviour.
  • If every channel is busy when a user calls, that user is blocked.
  • Trade-off: fewer channels \(\rightarrow\) cheaper, but more blocking.
Grade of service (GoS)
  • GoS \(=\) a measure of a user's ability to access the system during the busy hour.
  • Busy hour \(=\) the busiest hour of a week, month or year. For cellular it is typically 4 to 6 pm Thursday or Friday.
  • Stated either as
    • probability a call is blocked (Erlang B), or
    • probability a call is delayed beyond a set queuing time (Erlang C).
  • AMPS is designed for GoS \(=\) 2 % blocking: 2 calls in 100 are lost in the busy hour.
  • The designer's job: estimate peak demand, then allocate enough channels to meet the GoS.
Definitions (82 Bh asks for exactly these)
  • Set-up time: time to allocate a trunked channel to a requesting user.
  • Blocked call (lost call): a call that cannot be completed at the time of request, because of congestion.
  • Holding time \(H\): average duration of a typical call, in seconds.
  • Request rate \(\lambda\): average number of call requests per unit time.
  • Traffic intensity \(A\): average channel occupancy, in Erlangs. Dimensionless.
  • Load: traffic intensity across the whole system.
  • 1 Erlang \(=\) one channel occupied 100 % of the time (one call-hour per hour). Eg a channel busy for 30 min in an hour carries 0.5 Erlang.
The three traffic equations
  • Per user: \(A_u = \lambda H\)
  • Total offered, \(U\) users: \(A = U A_u\)
  • Per channel, \(C\) channels: \(A_c = U A_u / C\)
  • Offered traffic is not carried traffic. Once offered traffic exceeds capacity, the carried traffic saturates at \(C\) Erlangs.
The two types of trunked system
Blocked calls cleared \(\rightarrow\) Erlang B
  • No queue. A user who finds no free channel is refused and is free to try again.
  • Assumptions: Poisson arrivals, infinite users, memoryless arrivals, exponentially distributed holding time, finite channels. This is an M/M/m/m queue.
  • GoS \(=\) probability of blocking: \[ \Pr[\text{blocking}] \;=\; \frac{\dfrac{A^C}{C!}} {\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{C} \dfrac{A^k}{k!}} \;=\; \text{GoS} \]
  • Gives a conservative (pessimistic) estimate, since a finite-user model always predicts less blocking.
  • In the exam you are given an Erlang B table or chart, never asked to sum the series.
Blocked calls delayed \(\rightarrow\) Erlang C
  • A queue holds blocked calls until a channel frees up.
  • Probability a call is delayed at all: \[ \Pr[\text{delay} > 0] \;=\; \frac{A^C} {A^C + C!\left(1-\dfrac{A}{C}\right)\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{C-1}\dfrac{A^k}{k!}} \]
  • GoS \(=\) probability the delay exceeds \(t\) seconds: \[ \Pr[\text{delay} > t] = \Pr[\text{delay}>0]\;e^{-(C-A)t/H} \]
  • Average delay over all calls: \[ D = \Pr[\text{delay}>0]\;\frac{H}{C-A} \] where \(H/(C-A)\) is the average delay of those calls that were queued.
Trunking efficiency: a large trunked group carries far more traffic per channel than several small ones at the same GoS. This is why sectoring, which splits one channel pool into 3 or 6 smaller pools, always loses some trunking efficiency even though it improves SIR. (81 Ba asks for exactly this loss, 6)

column1: What techniques enhance capacity and coverage in a cellular radio network?
column4:
Why it is needed
  • A new system is deployed with few users, spread evenly \(\rightarrow\) demand is low.
  • As subscribers grow, demand in some cells exceeds what those BSs can carry.
  • More spectrum is not available \(\rightarrow\) capacity must come from geometry.
Cell splittingSectoringMicrocell zone
IdeaSubdivide a congested cell into smaller cellsReplace the omni antenna w/ directional antennasSplit a cell into zones fed by one BS
\(R\)ReducedUnchangedUnchanged
\(D/R\)UnchangedReduced (via smaller \(N\))Reduced
Gains capacity byMore clusters per unit areaAllowing a smaller \(N\)Allowing a smaller \(N\) w/o extra handoffs
HandoffsMore (smaller cells)Many more (sector to sector)None between zones
CostNew BSs, towers, real estateLoses trunking efficiencyZone sites plus fibre or microwave links
Cell splitting 5
  • Subdivide a congested cell into smaller cells, each w/ its own BS and reduced antenna height and transmit power.
  • New smaller cells are called microcells and are dropped in between the existing cells.
  • Halving \(R\) needs about 4 times as many cells to cover the same area (area \(\propto R^2\)).
  • More cells \(\rightarrow\) more clusters \(\rightarrow\) more channels per unit area \(\rightarrow\) higher capacity.
  • Cell splitting merely rescales the geometry: \(Q = D/R\) is unchanged, so the reuse plan still works.
The power reduction (commonly examined)
  • Received power must be equal at the old and new cell edges, so the reuse plan behaves the same: \[ P_r[\text{old edge}] \propto P_{t1} R^{-n}, \qquad P_r[\text{new edge}] \propto P_{t2} (R/2)^{-n} \]
  • Setting them equal w/ \(n=4\): \[ P_{t2} = \frac{P_{t1}}{16} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{\text{reduce transmit power by }12\text{ dB}} \]
Problems
  • In practice not all cells are split at once \(\rightarrow\) two cell sizes coexist.
  • Neither the old nor the new power works for both:
    • all-high power \(\rightarrow\) small cells break the co-channel separation,
    • all-low power \(\rightarrow\) parts of the large cells go unserved.
  • So channels must be split into two groups, one per cell size. The large cell takes high-speed traffic so it hands off less often.
  • Needs new towers and antennas, and lowers spectral efficiency during the transition.
Each original cell is surrounded by microcells of half the radius, placed so the reuse plan is preserved.
Sectoring 5
  • Keep \(R\) fixed, and instead attack \(D/R\).
  • Replace the single omni-directional BS antenna w/ several directional antennas, each radiating into one sector.
  • A cell is normally split into three \(120^\circ\) or six \(60^\circ\) sectors.
  • Each sector gets its own channel sub-group, used only in that sector.
  • A given cell now transmits to, and receives interference from, only a fraction of the co-channel cells.
Omni, \(120^\circ\), \(90^\circ\) and \(60^\circ\) sectoring.
The two-step gain (state it in this order)
  • Step 1: directional antennas cut the number of first-tier interferers.
    • omni \(\rightarrow\) 6 interferers,
    • \(120^\circ\) \(\rightarrow\) 2 interferers,
    • \(60^\circ\) \(\rightarrow\) 1 interferer.
  • SIR therefore improves (17 dB \(\rightarrow\) about 24.2 dB for \(120^\circ\)).
  • Step 2: spend that margin. Reduce \(N\) (eg \(7 \rightarrow 4\) or 3), which raises capacity, until SIR is back at the required value.
  • Note the transmit power is not reduced. Only the relative interference is.
Sector 0 receives interference only from sectors 4, 5 and 6, so the 6 interfering cells drop to 3 (2 in the exact Rappaport treatment for \(120^\circ\)).
Disadvantages
  • The cell's channels are split into 3 or 6 smaller pools \(\rightarrow\) trunking efficiency falls, so carried traffic drops for the same channel count.
  • Many more handoffs, one per sector crossing, loading the MSC.
  • More antennas per site.
Repeaters for range extension syllabus, no PYQ yet
  • Radio retransmitters used to cover hard-to-reach places: inside buildings, valleys, tunnels.
  • Bidirectional: receives from the serving BS, amplifies, reradiates into the target area, and does the same in reverse.
  • Works over the air \(\rightarrow\) can be installed anywhere, repeats a whole band.
  • Often feeds a distributed antenna system (DAS) inside a building.
  • A repeater adds coverage, not capacity. It only reradiates the BS signal.
  • It also reradiates the received noise and interference, so placement and gain settings need care.
Microcell zone concept 31+3
HOT 3 80 Ba, 81 Ba, 79 Ch  \(\cdot\) asked as “why do we need it?”, so lead with the problem
Why it is needed (the marked part)
  • Sectoring buys capacity but multiplies handoffs, one per sector boundary.
  • Every handoff loads the MSC and the control links.
  • Sectoring also loses trunking efficiency by splitting the channel pool.
  • The microcell zone concept buys the same capacity without either penalty.
Three zone sites (Tx/Rx), one base station, joined by fibre or microwave. A mobile crossing between zones keeps its channel.
How it works
  • A cell is divided into 3 or more zones, each w/ a zone site (Tx/Rx) placed at the outer edge of the cell.
  • All zone sites connect back to one single BS, by coaxial cable, fibre or microwave link, and share its radio equipment.
  • Each zone uses a directional antenna radiating inward.
  • The mobile is served by whichever zone is strongest.
  • Any BS channel may be assigned to any zone.
  • As the mobile crosses from zone to zone it keeps the same channel. The BS just switches which zone site radiates it, so no handoff reaches the MSC.
Result
  • A channel is live only in the zone the mobile is in \(\rightarrow\) radiation is localised \(\rightarrow\) interference falls.
  • \(D/R\) drops to about 3, so \(N\) can drop from 7 to 3.
  • Capacity rises about 2.33 times at the same 18 dB SIR requirement.
  • Particularly good along highways and urban traffic corridors.

  • SIR therefore improves (17 dB \(\rightarrow\) about 24.2 dB for \(120^\circ\)).
  • Step 2: spend that margin. Reduce \(N\) (eg \(7 \rightarrow 4\) or 3), which raises capacity, until SIR is back at the required value.
  • Note the transmit power is not reduced. Only the relative interference is.
Sector 0 receives interference only from sectors 4, 5 and 6, so the 6 interfering cells drop to 3 (2 in the exact Rappaport treatment for \(120^\circ\)).
Disadvantages
  • The cell's channels are split into 3 or 6 smaller pools \(\rightarrow\) trunking efficiency falls, so carried traffic drops for the same channel count.
  • Many more handoffs, one per sector crossing, loading the MSC.
  • More antennas per site.
Repeaters for range extension syllabus, no PYQ yet
  • Radio retransmitters used to cover hard-to-reach places: inside buildings, valleys, tunnels.
  • Bidirectional: receives from the serving BS, amplifies, reradiates into the target area, and does the same in reverse.
  • Works over the air \(\rightarrow\) can be installed anywhere, repeats a whole band.
  • Often feeds a distributed antenna system (DAS) inside a building.
  • A repeater adds coverage, not capacity. It only reradiates the BS signal.
  • It also reradiates the received noise and interference, so placement and gain settings need care.

column1: Microcell zone concept
column4:
Why it is needed (the marked part)
  • Sectoring buys capacity but multiplies handoffs, one per sector boundary.
  • Every handoff loads the MSC and the control links.
  • Sectoring also loses trunking efficiency by splitting the channel pool.
  • The microcell zone concept buys the same capacity without either penalty.
Three zone sites (Tx/Rx), one base station, joined by fibre or microwave. A mobile crossing between zones keeps its channel.
How it works
  • A cell is divided into 3 or more zones, each w/ a zone site (Tx/Rx) placed at the outer edge of the cell.
  • All zone sites connect back to one single BS, by coaxial cable, fibre or microwave link, and share its radio equipment.
  • Each zone uses a directional antenna radiating inward.
  • The mobile is served by whichever zone is strongest.
  • Any BS channel may be assigned to any zone.
  • As the mobile crosses from zone to zone it keeps the same channel. The BS just switches which zone site radiates it, so no handoff reaches the MSC.
Result
  • A channel is live only in the zone the mobile is in \(\rightarrow\) radiation is localised \(\rightarrow\) interference falls.
  • \(D/R\) drops to about 3, so \(N\) can drop from 7 to 3.
  • Capacity rises about 2.33 times at the same 18 dB SIR requirement.
  • Particularly good along highways and urban traffic corridors.

column1: Chapter 2 numericals — which formulas does everything come from?
column4:
Every problem below is a real PYQ, with its year tags and marks. Solutions are worked in full: what was calculated, why, and which formula was used. Nothing is skipped to save space.
The five formulas everything here is built on
  • Cluster size \(N = i^2 + ij + j^2\) (allowed: 1, 3, 4, 7, 9, 12, 13, 16, 19, 21)
  • Co-channel reuse ratio \(Q = D/R = \sqrt{3N}\)
  • Worst-case SIR \(\dfrac{S}{I} = \dfrac{(\sqrt{3N})^{\,n}}{i_0}\), so \(N = \dfrac{1}{3}\left(i_0 \cdot \dfrac{S}{I}\right)^{2/n}\)
  • Hexagonal cell area \(A = \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}R^2 = 2.598\,R^2\)
  • Traffic \(A_u = \lambda H\), \(A = U A_u\), and Erlang B for the GoS
\(i_0\) \(=\) number of first-tier interferers: 6 omni, 2 for \(120^\circ\) sectoring, 1 for \(60^\circ\) sectoring. \(n\) \(=\) path loss exponent.

column1: Problem 1  Prove \(Q=\sqrt{3N}\) and find the optimal \(N\) — 1.1   SIR \(=\) 15 dB worst case, \(n = 4\), considering trunking efficiency (71 Bh)
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2071 Bhadra · Q2 · [4+4]
Prove that for a hexagonal geometry the co-channel reuse ratio is given by \(Q = \sqrt{3N}\); Where \(N = i^2 + j^2 + ij\). A cellular service provider decides to use a digital TDMA scheme which can tolerate a Signal-to-Interference Ratio of 15 dB in the worst case. Find the optimal value of \(N\) for
  1. Omni directional antennas
  2. \(120^\circ\) Sectoring
  3. \(60^\circ\) Sectoring
[Use path loss exponent of 4 and consider trunking efficiency]
column4:
• Step 1: convert SIR to a linear ratio. The formula is in power ratio, not dB. \[ \frac{S}{I} = 10^{15/10} = 10^{1.5} = 31.6228 \]
  • Step 2: apply \(\;N = \frac{1}{3}\left(i_0 \cdot S/I\right)^{2/n}\;\) for each antenna configuration. Equivalently find \(Q\) first, then \(N = Q^2/3\).
Configuration\(i_0\)\(Q=(i_0\,S/I)^{1/n}\)\(N = Q^2/3\)Round up to allowed \(N\)
Omni-directional6\((6\times31.6228)^{1/4} = (189.74)^{0.25} = 3.7114\)\(3.7114^2/3 = 4.5915\)\(N=7\)
\(120^\circ\) sectoring2\((2\times31.6228)^{1/4} = (63.246)^{0.25} = 2.8201\)\(2.8201^2/3 = 2.6509\)\(N=3\)
\(60^\circ\) sectoring1\((31.6228)^{1/4} = 2.3714\)\(2.3714^2/3 = 1.8745\)\(N=3\)
  • Step 3: why round up, not to the nearest. \(N\) must be one of \(1,3,4,7,9,12,\dots\), and a smaller \(N\) gives a worse SIR. Rounding down would break the 15 dB requirement. So always take the next allowed value above the computed one.
    • omni: \(4.5915 \rightarrow\) next allowed is 7 (4 is allowed but \(4 < 4.5915\)),
    • \(120^\circ\): \(2.6509 \rightarrow 3\),
    • \(60^\circ\): \(1.8745 \rightarrow 3\).
  • Step 4: comment on the results (the marks for “considering trunking efficiency”).
    • Sectoring cuts the required cluster size from 7 to 3, so each cell keeps \(7/3 = 2.33\) times as many channels.
    • But \(60^\circ\) sectoring gives the same \(N=3\) as \(120^\circ\) here, while splitting each cell's channels into 6 pools instead of 3.
    • A pool of 6 smaller groups carries less traffic at the same GoS than 3 larger ones. So \(60^\circ\) buys no extra capacity and loses more trunking efficiency.
    • Conclusion: \(120^\circ\) sectoring with \(N=3\) is the best choice.

column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2079 Bhadra · Q2 · [3+5]
Define Grade of Service (GoS) and explain how can it be measured in a `blocked call cleared' type of trunking system. A cellular service provider decides to use a digital TDMA scheme that can tolerate a signal-to-interference ratio of 15 dB in the worst case. The mobile radio channel provided a propagation path loss exponent of \(n = 3\). Find the optimal value of \(N\) for (a) Omni-directional antennas, (b) 1200 sectoring, and Ic) \(60^\circ\) sectoring. Comment on your results. “1200 sectoring” and “Ic)” are the paper's own typos for \(120^\circ\) and (c).
column4:
• Same \(S/I = 31.6228\), but now the exponent is \(2/n = 2/3\).
Configuration\(i_0\)\(Q=(i_0\,S/I)^{1/3}\)\(N = Q^2/3\)Round up
Omni6\((189.74)^{1/3} = 5.7462\)\(5.7462^2/3 = 11.0064\)\(N=12\)
\(120^\circ\)2\((63.246)^{1/3} = 3.9842\)\(3.9842^2/3 = 5.2913\)\(N=7\)
\(60^\circ\)1\((31.6228)^{1/3} = 3.1623\)\(3.1623^2/3 = 3.3333\)\(N=4\)
  • Comment. A smaller path loss exponent means interference decays more slowly, so co-channel cells must sit further apart and \(N\) rises sharply (\(7 \rightarrow 12\) for omni).
  • Sectoring is therefore even more valuable in a low-\(n\) environment: it takes \(N\) from 12 down to 4, a \(3\times\) capacity gain.

column1: Problem 1  Prove \(Q=\sqrt{3N}\) and find the optimal \(N\) — 1.4   Exact Vs approximate SIR for \(N=7\), \(n=4\)
column3:
PROBLEM not a PYQ · the follow-up every examiner likes verified/added
For a 7-cell cluster with \(n = 4\), compute the worst-case \(S/I\) twice: first with the approximation that all six first-tier interferers lie at the same distance \(D\), and then exactly, with a mobile at the cell edge seeing interferers at \(D-R\), \(D\), \(D\), \(D\), \(D\) and \(D+R\). Compare the two, in dB.
column4:
• Approximate (all six interferers taken at distance \(D\)): \[ \frac{S}{I} = \frac{(\sqrt{3\times7})^{4}}{6} = \frac{4.5826^4}{6} = \frac{441.0}{6} = 73.50 \;=\; 18.66\ \text{dB} \]
  • Exact (mobile at the cell edge, true distances \(D-R,\,D,\,D,\,D,\,D,\,D+R\) with \(Q = D/R = 4.5826\)): \[ \frac{S}{I} = \frac{1}{2(Q-1)^{-4} + 2(Q+1)^{-4} + 2Q^{-4}} = 53.376 \;=\; 17.27\ \text{dB} \]
  • The approximation is optimistic by about 1.4 dB. Both fall short of the 18 dB AMPS target, which is the standard justification for sectoring.

column1: Problem 2  Spectrum, duplex channels and channels per cell
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2070 Bhadra · Q2 · [3+4+3]
Explain the difference between co-channel and adjacent channel interference. Prove that the co-channel reuse ratio is given by \(Q = \sqrt{3N}\), where \(N = i^2 + ij + j^2\) is the cluster size. If 20 MHz of total spectrum is allocated for a duplex (i.e. bidirectional) wireless cellular system and each simplex (i.e. one-way) channel has 25 KHz of bandwidth, find
  1. The number of duplex channels, and
  2. The total number of channels per cell, assuming a cluster size of \(N = 4\).
column4:
The \(Q=\sqrt{3N}\) proof is Problem 1 above; only the spectrum arithmetic is new here.
  • Step 1: what one duplex channel actually costs. A duplex (two-way) channel needs two simplex channels, one for each direction. \[ B_{\text{duplex}} = 2 \times 25\ \text{kHz} = 50\ \text{kHz} \] Missing this factor of 2 is the single most common error in this question.
  • Step 2: total duplex channels. \[ N_{\text{total}} = \frac{20 \times 10^{6}}{50 \times 10^{3}} = \boxed{400\ \text{duplex channels}} \]
  • Step 3: channels per cell for \(N = 4\). \[ k = \frac{S}{N} = \frac{400}{4} = \boxed{100\ \text{channels per cell}} \]
  • Step 4: the other cluster sizes, for comparison.
    • \(N = 7\): \(\;400/7 = 57.14 \rightarrow 57\) channels per cell,
    • \(N = 12\): \(\;400/12 = 33.33 \rightarrow 33\) channels per cell.
  • Always round down here: a fractional channel cannot be allocated.

column1: Problem 3  Minimum co-channel distance from the cell area
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2074 Bhadra · Q2 (b) · [4]
For a seven cell reuse pattern, find the minimum distance between centers of co-channel cells. Area of each cell is uniform and is equal to 23 square km.
column4:
• Step 1: get \(R\) from the area. The cell is a regular hexagon of “radius” \(R\) (centre to vertex), so \[ A = \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}R^2 = 2.598\,R^2 \] \[ R = \sqrt{\frac{A}{2.598}} = \sqrt{\frac{23}{2.598}} = \sqrt{8.8530} = 2.9754\ \text{km} \]
  • Step 2: apply the reuse ratio. For \(N = 7\), \[ Q = \sqrt{3N} = \sqrt{21} = 4.5826 \]
  • Step 3: minimum co-channel distance. \[ D = Q \cdot R = 4.5826 \times 2.9754 = \boxed{13.635\ \text{km}} \]
  • Sanity check. \(D/R = 13.635/2.9754 = 4.58\) ✓matches \(\sqrt{21}\).
  • If the question had given the area as a circle instead, use \(A = \pi R^2\) and \(R = \sqrt{23/\pi} = 2.7052\) km, giving \(D = 12.397\) km. Read the wording carefully: “uniform cell” in this paper means the hexagon.

column1: Problem 4  Users supported and market penetration
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2080 Baishakh · Q2 (a) · [5] · 2079 Chaitra · Q2 (a) · [5]
An urban area has a population of two million residents. System A has 394 cells with 19 channels each. Find the number of users that can be supported at 2% blocking if each user average two calls per hour at average call duration of three minutes. Assuming that trunk systems are operated at maximum capacity, compute the percentage market penetration of cellular provider. Both papers print this word for word (79 Ch reads “averages two calls”), and 79 Ch attaches the Erlang B table with the \(N = 19\) row: 11.23 at 1%, 12.33 at 2%.
column4:
• Step 1: traffic intensity per user. \(\;A_u = \lambda H\), and both terms must be in the same time unit. \[ \lambda = 2\ \text{calls/hour}, \qquad H = 3\ \text{min} = \frac{3}{60}\ \text{hour} \] \[ A_u = 2 \times \frac{3}{60} = \boxed{0.1\ \text{Erlang per user}} \]
  • Step 2: carried traffic per cell, from the Erlang B table. With \(C = 19\) channels and GoS \(=\) 0.02, \[ A = 12\ \text{Erlang} \] (The exact Erlang B value is 12.333 Erlang; the standard table rounds to 12, which is what the marking scheme expects.)
  • Step 3: users per cell. \[ U = \frac{A}{A_u} = \frac{12}{0.1} = 120\ \text{users per cell} \]
  • Step 4: total subscribers. \[ U_{\text{total}} = 120 \times 394 = \boxed{47\,280\ \text{subscribers}} \]
  • Step 5: market penetration. \[ \frac{47\,280}{2\,000\,000} = 0.02364 = \boxed{2.364\ \%} \]
  • Note the assumption stated in the question: “trunked systems operate at maximum capacity”. That is what allows the full 12 Erlang per cell to be used.
  • Using the exact 12.333 Erlang instead gives 123.33 users/cell, 48 592 subscribers and 2.430 % penetration. Either is acceptable if the table value used is stated.

• (a) Traffic intensity per user. \[ A_u = \lambda H = 3 \times \frac{5}{60} = \boxed{0.25\ \text{Erlang}} \]
  • (b) One channel, GoS \(=\) 1 %. From the printed table, \(C = 1\) and \(B = 1\,\%\) give \(A = 0.010\) Erlang. \[ U = \frac{A}{A_u} = \frac{0.010}{0.25} = 0.04\ \text{users} \] \[ \Rightarrow \boxed{0\ \text{users}} \] Interpretation: a single channel cannot support even one such user at 1 % blocking. A lone user offering 0.25 Erlang to one channel would be blocked about \(0.25/(1+0.25) = 20\,\%\) of the time.
  • (c) Five trunked channels, GoS \(=\) 1 %. From the table, \(C = 5\) and \(B = 1\,\%\) give \(A = 1.36\) Erlang. \[ U = \frac{1.36}{0.25} = 5.44 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{5\ \text{users}} \]

  • (d) Users doubled to 10. \[ A = U A_u = 10 \times 0.25 = 2.5\ \text{Erlang} \] Apply the Erlang B formula with \(C = 5\), \(A = 2.5\): \[ \Pr[\text{blocking}] = \frac{A^C/C!}{\sum_{k=0}^{C} A^k/k!} \]

    \[ \sum_{k=0}^{5} \frac{A^k}{k!} = 11.6706, \qquad \Pr[\text{blocking}] = \frac{0.8138}{11.6706} = 0.0697 \] \[ \boxed{\text{GoS} = 6.97\ \% } \]

column1: Problem 6  Full system design from area and spectrum
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2072 Magh · Q2 · [12]
A city with a coverage area of 1500 sq km is covered with a 12-cell system each with a radius of 1.387 km. If the total spectrum allocated is 28.5 MHz with a full duplex channel bandwidth of 25 MHz. Assume a GOS of 0.02 for a blocked calls cleared system, is specified and the offered traffic per user is 0.03 Erlangs and traffic intensity of each cell is 84 Erlang, compute:
  1. the number of cells in the service area
  2. the number of channels per cell
  3. the maximum carrier traffic
  4. the total number of users that can be served for 2% GOS
  5. the number of mobiles per unique channel.
  6. Theoretical maximum number of users that could be served at one time by the system.
The paper prints “25 MHz” for the channel bandwidth: a typo for 25 kHz, since 28.5 MHz would otherwise buy one channel. Solve with 25 kHz and say so.
column4:
• (a) Number of cells in the service area. \[ A_{\text{cell}} = 2.598\,R^2 = 2.598 \times (1.387)^2 = 2.598 \times 1.9238 = 4.998\ \text{km}^2 \] \[ n_{\text{cells}} = \frac{1500}{4.998} = 300.12 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{300\ \text{cells}} \]
  • (b) Channels per cell. \[ N_{\text{total}} = \frac{28.5 \times 10^{6}}{25 \times 10^{3}} = 1140\ \text{duplex channels} \] The question says “full duplex channel bandwidth 25 kHz”, so the \(\times 2\) of Problem 2 does not apply here. Read the wording. \[ k = \frac{1140}{12} = \boxed{95\ \text{channels per cell}} \]
  • (c) Maximum carried traffic per cell. The question supplies this as 84 Erlang. Cross-check from Erlang B: \(C = 95\) at GoS \(=\) 0.02 gives \(A = 83.13\) Erlang, so the given 84 is consistent. \[ A_{\text{cell}} = \boxed{84\ \text{Erlang}} \] System total \(= 84 \times 300 = 25\,200\) Erlang.
  • (d) Total users served at 2 % GoS. \[ U_{\text{cell}} = \frac{A_{\text{cell}}}{A_u} = \frac{84}{0.03} = 2800 \ \text{users per cell} \] \[ U_{\text{total}} = 2800 \times 300 = \boxed{840\,000\ \text{users}} \]
  • (e) Mobiles per unique channel. \[ \frac{U_{\text{cell}}}{k} = \frac{2800}{95} = \boxed{29.47\ \text{mobiles per channel}} \] Ie roughly 29 subscribers share each radio channel, which is exactly the statistical multiplexing gain trunking delivers.
  • (f) Theoretical maximum users served at one time. Every channel in every cell busy simultaneously: \[ 95 \times 300 = \boxed{28\,500\ \text{simultaneous calls}} \]
  • Sanity check on (d) against (f): 840 000 subscribers share 28 500 simultaneous circuits, a ratio of 29.5:1, matching (e). ✓

column1: Problem 7  Area, channels and simultaneous calls
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2082 Bhadra · Q2 (b) · [4]
The cellular system has 32 cells, each cell has a 1.6 km radius and the system reuse factor is 7. The system is to support 336 traffic channels in total. Determine the total geographical area covered, the number of traffic channels per cell and the total number of simultaneous calls supported by this system.
column4:
• Step 1: area of one cell. \[ A_{\text{cell}} = 2.598 \times (1.6)^2 = 2.598 \times 2.56 = 6.6509\ \text{km}^2 \]
  • Step 2: total geographical area. \[ A_{\text{total}} = 32 \times 6.6509 = \boxed{212.83\ \text{km}^2} \]
  • Step 3: channels per cell. \[ k = \frac{S}{N} = \frac{336}{7} = \boxed{48\ \text{channels per cell}} \]
  • Step 4: simultaneous calls. Every cell can run all 48 of its channels at once, and there are 32 cells: \[ 48 \times 32 = \boxed{1536\ \text{simultaneous calls}} \]
  • Watch the trap: the 336 channels are the system total, reused by every cluster. The system supports 1536 calls, not 336, because the cluster repeats \(32/7 = 4.57\) times.

column1: Problem 8  Trunking loss from omni to \(60^\circ\) sectoring
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2081 Baishakh · Q2 (a) · [2+2+2]
For a cluster \(N = 7\) system with a blocking probability of 1% and an average call length of two minutes, find the traffic capacity loss for a blocked calls cleared system due to trunking for 57 channels when going from omnidirectional antennas to \(60^\circ\) sectored antennas. The average request rate per user is 1 call per hour.
GOS / Channel0.5%1%2%
1.005.0101.0204
93.3333.7834.345

column4:
• Step 1: traffic per user. \[ A_u = \lambda H = 1 \times \frac{2}{60} = 0.0333\ \text{Erlang} \]
  • Step 2: omni-directional case. All 57 channels sit in one trunked pool. From the table, \(C = 57\) at 1 % gives \[ A_{\text{omni}} = 44.2\ \text{Erlang} \] \[ U_{\text{omni}} = \frac{44.2}{0.0333} = 1326\ \text{users per cell} \]
  • Step 3: \(60^\circ\) sectored case. The cell is split into 6 sectors, and each sector gets its own channel group: \[ \frac{57}{6} = 9.5 \;\Rightarrow\; 9\ \text{channels per sector} \] Round down: a channel cannot be split between sectors. From the table, \(C = 9\) at 1 % gives \(A = 3.783\) Erlang per sector, so \[ A_{\text{sectored}} = 6 \times 3.783 = 22.698\ \text{Erlang} \] \[ U_{\text{sectored}} = \frac{22.698}{0.0333} = 681\ \text{users per cell} \]
  • Step 4: the loss. \[ \Delta A = 44.2 - 22.698 = \boxed{21.50\ \text{Erlang lost}} \] \[ \frac{21.50}{44.2} \times 100 = \boxed{48.65\ \% \text{ capacity loss}} \]
  • Why this happens (state this, it is where the marks are).
    • Erlang B is strongly non-linear in the channel count. One pool of 57 channels carries 44.2 Erlang, but six pools of 9 carry only \(6 \times 3.783 = 22.7\) Erlang.
    • That is the loss of trunking efficiency: a large pool absorbs random peaks far better than several small ones.
    • Three channels are also lost outright to the rounding (\(57 \rightarrow 6 \times 9 = 54\)).
  • The complete engineering picture: sectoring improves SIR, which lets \(N\) be reduced, which gives more channels per cell. That gain must beat the 48.65 % trunking loss computed here, otherwise sectoring is a net loss. This problem deliberately shows only the cost side.

column1: Problem 9  Calls per cell per hour, and SIR
column3:
PROBLEM not a PYQ · lecture-note example verified/added
A cellular system has 416 radio channels available, of which 21 are control channels. The average channel holding time is 3 minutes and the blocking probability during the busy hour is 2%. The frequency reuse factor is 9. Find (i) the number of calls per cell per hour, and (ii) the signal to co-channel interference ratio in dB (take \(n = 4\)).
column4:
• Step 1: voice channels. \[ 416 - 21 = 395\ \text{voice channels} \]
  • Step 2: voice channels per cell. \[ \frac{395}{9} = 43.89 \;\Rightarrow\; 44\ \text{channels per cell} \ \text{(taken as 44 for the table lookup)} \]
  • Step 3: carried traffic. From the Erlang B table, \(C = 44\) at GoS \(=\) 0.02 gives \[ A = 34.683\ \text{Erlang} \]
  • Step 4: convert Erlang to calls. 1 Erlang \(=\) one continuously occupied channel. With a 3-minute holding time, one Erlang carries \(1/3\) call per minute. \[ \text{calls per cell per minute} = \frac{34.683}{3} = 11.561 \] \[ \text{calls per cell per hour} = 11.561 \times 60 = \boxed{694\ \text{calls/cell/hour}} \]
  • Step 5: SIR for \(N = 9\), \(n = 4\). \[ Q = \sqrt{3 \times 9} = \sqrt{27} = 5.1962 \] \[ \frac{S}{I} = \frac{Q^4}{6} = \frac{729}{6} = 121.5 \] \[ \frac{S}{I}\,[\text{dB}] = 10\log_{10}(121.5) = \boxed{20.85\ \text{dB}} \]
  • Comment: 20.85 dB comfortably exceeds the 18 dB AMPS requirement, so \(N=9\) is a conservative, high-quality plan. \(N=7\) would give 18.66 dB, barely adequate.

column1: Problem 10  Cell splitting: the transmit power reduction
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2081 Bhadra · Q3 · [4] · 2075 Bhadra · Q3 · [5]
A telephone network company needs to expand its capacity based on demand on a city. A group of engineers was selected to find the solution. Among the solution sectoring and cell splitting were major technique for expansion purpose. Being a cellular planning engineer, which option do you think is best and why?
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2073 Bhadra · Q2 (a) · [5]
Explain how cell splitting and sectoring improve coverage and capacity in cellular system?
column4:
No paper prints numbers for this. The transmit-power result below is the only computable part, and it is what turns a prose answer into a full-mark one. verified/added
  • Requirement. The new microcell of radius \(R/2\) must deliver the same received power at its own boundary as the old cell did at its boundary. Only then does the reuse plan carry over unchanged.
  • Step 1: write both boundary powers. \[ P_r[\text{old boundary}] \propto P_{t1} R^{-n}, \qquad P_r[\text{new boundary}] \propto P_{t2} \left(\frac{R}{2}\right)^{-n} \]
  • Step 2: set them equal. \[ P_{t1} R^{-n} = P_{t2} \left(\frac{R}{2}\right)^{-n} \;\Longrightarrow\; \frac{P_{t2}}{P_{t1}} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{n} \]
  • Step 3: put \(n = 4\). \[ \frac{P_{t2}}{P_{t1}} = \frac{1}{16} = 0.0625 \] \[ 10\log_{10}(0.0625) = \boxed{-12.04\ \text{dB}, \text{ ie reduce power by 12 dB}} \]
  • Capacity effect. Halving \(R\) needs about 4 times as many cells (\(A \propto R^2\)), so the number of clusters, and therefore the capacity, rises about 4 times for the same spectrum.

column1: Problem 11  Cellular Vs non-cellular channel count
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2082 Baishakh · Q3 · [1+3]
Consider a single high-power transmitter that can support 40 voice channels over an area of 140 km² with the available spectrum. If this area is equally divided into seven smaller cells, each supported by lower power transmitters so that each cell supports 30% of the total voice channels, then determine
  1. Coverage area of each cell
  2. Total number of voice channels available in a cellular system compared to a non-cellular system.
column4:
• Step 1: coverage area of each cell. The 140 km² is divided equally into seven cells, so \[ A_{\text{cell}} = \frac{140}{7} = \boxed{20\ \text{km}^2} \]
  • Step 2: channels carried by one cell. Each cell supports 30 % of the total 40 voice channels — not 30 % of a share of them: \[ C_{\text{cell}} = 0.30 \times 40 = 12\ \text{channels} \]
  • Step 3: total channels in the cellular system. \[ C_{\text{cellular}} = 7 \times 12 = \boxed{84\ \text{voice channels}} \]
  • Step 4: compare with the non-cellular system. The single high-power transmitter carried only its 40 channels over the whole 140 km², so \[ \frac{C_{\text{cellular}}}{C_{\text{non-cellular}}} = \frac{84}{40} = \boxed{2.1\ \text{times}, \text{ ie 44 extra channels}} \]
  • This is frequency reuse in one line: the same 40 channels, re-used across seven lower-power cells, carry more than twice the traffic without one extra hertz of spectrum. The cost is seven base stations instead of one, plus handoff.
  • Watch the 30 %. Taking it as 30 % of \(40/7\) instead of 30 % of 40 gives \(7 \times 1.71 = 12\) channels total, which would make the cellular system worse than the single transmitter — a clear sign the reading is wrong.

column1: Explain free space propagation. Relate radiated power to electric field
column4:
When it applies
  • Used to predict received signal strength when Tx and Rx have a clear, unobstructed LOS path.
  • Eg satellite links, microwave LOS links.
  • Almost never true for a mobile in a city, but every other model is built as a correction to it.
Step 1: power flux density
  • An isotropic source radiates \(P_t\) uniformly over a sphere of area \(4\pi d^2\).
  • Power flux density at distance \(d\): \[ P_d \;=\; \frac{P_t G_t}{4\pi d^2} \quad \text{W/m}^2 \]
  • EIRP \(= P_t G_t\) watts: the power an isotropic antenna would need to give the same reading in the main beam.
  • ERP uses a half-wave dipole as the reference instead: \(\text{ERP} = \text{EIRP} - 2.15\) dB.
Step 2: effective aperture
  • Effective aperture \(A_e\) \(=\) ratio of power available at the antenna terminals to the incident power per unit area. \[ A_e \;=\; \frac{G_r \lambda^2}{4\pi}, \qquad \lambda = \frac{c}{f} \]
Step 3: the Friis equation
  • \(P_r = P_d \cdot A_e\), so \[ \boxed{\;P_r(d) \;=\; \frac{P_t G_t G_r \lambda^2}{(4\pi)^2 d^2 L}\;} \]
  • \(L \ge 1\) \(=\) system loss (feeder attenuation, filters, mismatch). \(L=1\) means no hardware loss.
  • \(P_r \propto 1/d^2\) and \(\propto \lambda^2\): doubling distance costs 6 dB, doubling frequency costs 6 dB.
Path loss
  • With antenna gains: \[ PL(\text{dB}) = 10\log\frac{P_t}{P_r} = -10\log\!\left[\frac{G_t G_r \lambda^2}{(4\pi)^2 d^2}\right] \]
  • Without antenna gains (\(G_t = G_r = 1\)): \[ PL(\text{dB}) = -10\log\!\left[\frac{\lambda^2}{(4\pi)^2 d^2}\right] \]
  • Useful dB form, \(d\) in km and \(f\) in MHz: \[ PL_{\text{FS}} = 32.44 + 20\log f_{\text{MHz}} + 20\log d_{\text{km}} \] verified/added
  • The minus sign on the gain term says that term is a gain. The \((4\pi d/\lambda)^2\) term is the free space loss proper.
  • Raising \(d\) raises the loss, which pushes designers to lower frequencies to keep the link budget manageable.
Relating power to E-field (the 78 Ch / 80 Ba style numerical)
  • Power flux density in terms of the field: \[ P_d \;=\; \frac{|E|^2}{\eta} \;=\; \frac{|E|^2}{120\pi}, \qquad \eta = 377\;\Omega \text{ (free space)} \]
  • So \(E\) falls as \(1/d\) while power falls as \(1/d^2\).
  • Received power through the aperture: \[ P_r(d) \;=\; \frac{|E|^2}{120\pi}\cdot \frac{G_r\lambda^2}{4\pi} \]
  • rms voltage into a matched receiver of input resistance \(R_{\text{ant}}\): \[ P_r = \frac{V_{\text{rms}}^2}{R_{\text{ant}}} = \frac{(V_{\text{ant}}/2)^2}{R_{\text{ant}}} \;\Longrightarrow\; V_{\text{ant}} = 2\sqrt{P_r R_{\text{ant}}} \] The factor 2 is the matched-load voltage divider. Losing it is the standard mistake.
Far field (Fraunhofer region)
  • Friis is valid only beyond the far-field distance \[ d_f \;=\; \frac{2D^2}{\lambda} \] where \(D\) \(=\) the largest physical linear dimension of the antenna.
  • Also needs \(d_f \gg D\) and \(d_f \gg \lambda\).
  • The equation blows up at \(d = 0\), so a close-in reference distance \(d_0\) is used: \[ P_r(d) = P_r(d_0)\left(\frac{d_0}{d}\right)^2, \qquad d \ge d_0 \ge d_f \]
  • \(d_0\) is typically 1 km for large cells, 100 m for microcells, 1 m indoors.

column1: Explain the three basic radio wave propagation mechanisms. Large scale Vs small scale model
column4:
• Apart from the direct wave, the receiver gets reflected, diffracted and scattered waves.
  • They add vectorially, so the resultant varies in strength in real time. That is the physical origin of fading.
1. Reflection
  • Wave hits an object very large compared to the wavelength.
  • Eg the earth's surface, buildings, walls.
  • Part reflects, part transmits into the object.
  • Strength set by the reflection coefficient \(\Gamma\), which depends on polarisation, angle of incidence and the material.
  • At grazing incidence \(\Gamma \rightarrow -1\), ie full reflection with a \(180^\circ\) phase flip. That is the assumption the two-ray model rests on.
Knife-edge diffraction geometry. Effective obstruction height \(h\), distances \(d_1\) and \(d_2\) from Tx and Rx.
2. Diffraction (79 Bh pairs this with a Fresnel derivation, 2+6)
  • Path is obstructed by a surface with sharp edges.
  • Secondary waves bend around the obstacle into the shadow region.
  • This is what lets a mobile work with no LOS at all in urban and hilly terrain.
  • Explained by Huygens' principle: every point on a wavefront acts as a point source of secondary wavelets, which add to form the new front.
  • Diffraction loss grows as the obstruction fills more of the first Fresnel zone.
3. Scattering
  • Medium contains objects small compared to the wavelength, or rough surfaces.
  • Eg foliage, street signs, lamp posts, rain drops, snow.
  • Energy is spread in many directions.
  • Follows the same principles as diffraction.
  • Received signal is often stronger than reflection and diffraction alone predict, because scattering fills in the gaps.
Fresnel zones and the diffraction parameter
  • A Fresnel zone is the ellipsoid of revolution over which secondary waves reach the receiver with an excess path of \(n\lambda/2\).
  • Numbered \(F_1, F_2, F_3, \dots\). Odd zones add constructively, even zones destructively.
  • Size set by frequency and Tx–Rx distance.
  • Fresnel–Kirchhoff diffraction parameter \[ v \;=\; h\sqrt{\frac{2(d_1+d_2)}{\lambda d_1 d_2}} \]
  • Radius of the \(n\)-th zone at distance \(d_1\): \[ r_n = \sqrt{\frac{n\lambda d_1 d_2}{d_1+d_2}} \] verified/added
  • Rule of thumb: keep 55 % of the first Fresnel zone clear and the link behaves as free space.
  • Diffraction gain \(G_d\) (dB) against \(v\):
    • \(v \le -1\): \(G_d = 0\)
    • \(-1 \le v \le 0\): \(G_d = 20\log(0.5 - 0.62v)\)
    • \(0 \le v \le 1\): \(G_d = 20\log(0.5\,e^{-0.95v})\)
    • \(v > 2.4\): \(G_d = 20\log(0.225/v)\)
First and second Fresnel zones.

column1: Derive the path difference and phase difference in the two-ray model, and the path loss
column4:
Why it beats the free space model (the 2-mark opener)
  • Free space assumes one path. A real mobile link always has a ground-reflected path as well.
  • The two-ray model adds that second path, so it predicts the \(1/d^4\) roll-off actually measured over large distances, instead of \(1/d^2\).
  • Found reasonably accurate for large-cell mobile systems over a few km.
  • Needs no measured data, unlike Okumura or Hata.
Assumptions
  • \(h_t, h_r \gg \lambda\) and \(h_t, h_r \ll d\).
  • Reflected wave arrives at grazing incidence, so \(\Gamma = -1\).
  • Flat earth, no curvature.
Step 1: path difference \(\Delta\) (method of images)
  • Replace the reflection by an image transmitter at \(-h_t\).
  • LOS path and reflected path become two straight lines: \[ d' = \sqrt{(h_t-h_r)^2 + d^2}, \qquad d'' = \sqrt{(h_t+h_r)^2 + d^2} \]
  • So \[ \Delta = d''-d' = d\sqrt{1+\left(\tfrac{h_t+h_r}{d}\right)^2} - d\sqrt{1+\left(\tfrac{h_t-h_r}{d}\right)^2} \]
  • Expand each root binomially, valid since \(d \gg h_t,h_r\): \[ \Delta \approx d\left\{\left(1+\tfrac{1}{2}\left(\tfrac{h_t+h_r}{d}\right)^2\right) -\left(1+\tfrac{1}{2}\left(\tfrac{h_t-h_r}{d}\right)^2\right)\right\} \] \[ \boxed{\;\Delta \;\approx\; \frac{2 h_t h_r}{d}\;} \]
Method of images: the ground-reflected ray is redrawn as a straight line from the image transmitter at \(-h_t\).
Step 2: phase difference and time delay
\[ \boxed{\;\theta_\Delta = \frac{2\pi\Delta}{\lambda} = \frac{4\pi h_t h_r}{\lambda d}\;} \] \[ \tau_d = \frac{\Delta}{c} = \frac{\theta_\Delta}{2\pi f_c} \]
Step 3: total E-field
  • For large \(d\), \(|E_0 d_0 / d'| \approx |E_0 d_0 / d''| \approx |E_0 d_0 / d|\), so the two rays differ only in phase: \[ |E_{\text{tot}}(d)| = \frac{E_0 d_0}{d}\left|\cos\theta_\Delta - \cos 0\right| \]
  • Using \(\cos\alpha - \cos\beta\) identity: \[ |E_{\text{tot}}(d)| = 2\,\frac{E_0 d_0}{d}\,\sin\!\left(\frac{\theta_\Delta}{2}\right) \]
  • For \(\theta_\Delta/2 < 0.3\) rad, \(\sin x \approx x\): \[ \boxed{\;|E_{\text{tot}}(d)| \approx \frac{2 E_0 d_0}{d}\cdot \frac{2\pi h_t h_r}{\lambda d} = \frac{k}{d^2}\;} \]
  • The field now falls as \(1/d^2\), so power falls as \(1/d^4\).
Step 4: received power and path loss
  • Using \(P_r = |E_{\text{tot}}|^2 A_e / \eta\): \[ \boxed{\;P_r \;=\; P_t G_t G_r \frac{h_t^2 h_r^2}{d^4}\;} \]
  • Note \(\lambda\) has cancelled: the two-ray result is independent of frequency.
  • In dB: \[ \begin{gathered} PL(\text{dB}) = 40\log d \\ -\left(10\log G_t + 10\log G_r + 20\log h_t + 20\log h_r\right) \end{gathered} \]
  • Valid only beyond the crossover distance \(d_c = 4\pi h_t h_r/\lambda\); below it the model oscillates and free space is used instead. verified/added

column1: Explain the log-distance path loss model and log-normal shadowing
column4:
Log-distance path loss model
  • Both theory and measurement show received power falls logarithmically with distance, indoors and outdoors.
  • Generalises free space by letting the exponent be \(n\) instead of 2: \[ \overline{PL}(d) \propto \left(\frac{d}{d_0}\right)^{n} \] \[ \boxed{\;\overline{PL}(d)\,[\text{dB}] = \overline{PL}(d_0) + 10\,n\log\!\left(\frac{d}{d_0}\right)\;} \]
  • \(\overline{PL}(d_0)\) is computed by the free space formula, or measured.
  • Bars mean ensemble average over all possible paths at that distance.
  • One number, \(n\), absorbs the whole environment.
Link budget design
  • A link budget adds every gain and subtracts every loss between transmitter output and receiver input, then compares against the receiver sensitivity.
  • Generic form, all terms in dB: \[ P_r = P_t + G_t + G_r - L_{\text{cable,t}} - L_{\text{cable,r}} - L_{\text{misc}} - PL(d) \]
  • Link closes if \(P_r \ge\) sensitivity \(+\) link margin.
  • Two budgets are needed, forward and reverse, and the weaker one sets the cell radius.
How to run the exam version
  • Compute maximum allowable path loss on each link: \[ PL_{\max} = P_t + G_t + G_r - L_{\text{cables}} - \text{sensitivity} - \text{margin} \]
  • Put \(PL_{\max}\) into the propagation model given (usually Okumura) and solve for \(d\).
  • Take the smaller of the forward and reverse distances.
  • Compare against the range asked for and state whether the link is feasible.
Log-normal shadowing
  • Problem: two locations at the same \(d\) can have wildly different surroundings, so a single average is wrong for any one site.
  • Measurement shows \(PL(d)\) at a given \(d\) is random, and log-normally distributed about the average.
  • Add a zero-mean Gaussian random variable \(X_\sigma\) in dB, standard deviation \(\sigma\) dB: \[ \boxed{\;PL(d) = \overline{PL}(d_0) + 10 n \log\!\left(\frac{d}{d_0}\right) + X_\sigma\;} \] \[ P_r(d)\,[\text{dBm}] = P_t\,[\text{dBm}] - PL(d) \]
  • Called shadowing: the mobile is shadowed by clutter (buildings, hills, foliage).
  • \(n\) and \(\sigma\) are found from measured data by linear regression, minimising mean square error.
  • Small \(\sigma\) \(=\) the model fits that environment well.
Two ways to build a propagation model
  • Empirical: collect measurements, fit curves. Eg Okumura, Hata.
    • Accurate in the environment measured, no guarantee elsewhere.
  • Analytical: model the physics, derive equations. Eg free space, two-ray.
    • Purely analytical models are inaccurate because so many assumptions are needed to keep the derivation tractable.
  • Practical models are hybrids: an analytical core with measured correction factors.
