column1: Explain any two outdoor propagation models. State the conditions for Okumura and Hata
column4:
Outdoor transmission runs over irregular terrain, so the terrain profile, trees, buildings and hills must all be accounted for. Purely analytical models cannot do this, so all the outdoor models below are empirical.
Okumura model 4
  • Wholly empirical. Built from extensive drive-test measurements in and around Tokyo, 1968.
  • The single most widely used model for signal prediction in urban areas.
  • Okumura published a set of curves of median attenuation relative to free space, \(A_{mu}(f,d)\), for an urban area over quasi-smooth terrain, plus correction curves.
  • Validity conditions (the 2-mark answer)
    • Frequency 150 MHz to 1920 MHz (extrapolated to 3 GHz).
    • Distance 1 km to 100 km.
    • BS antenna height 30 m to 1000 m.
    • Quasi-smooth terrain, urban reference.
  • The formula \[ \boxed{\;L_{50}(\text{dB}) = L_F + A_{mu}(f,d) - G(h_{te}) - G(h_{re}) - G_{\text{AREA}}\;} \]
    • \(L_{50}\) \(=\) median (50th percentile) path loss,
    • \(L_F\) \(=\) free space path loss,
    • \(A_{mu}\) \(=\) median attenuation relative to free space, read off the curve,
    • \(G(h_{te}), G(h_{re})\) \(=\) antenna height gain factors,
    • \(G_{\text{AREA}}\) \(=\) gain from the environment type.
\(A_{mu}(f,d)\) over a quasi-smooth urban area, \(h_{te} = 200\) m, \(h_{re} = 3\) m.
  • Height gain factors: \[ G(h_{te}) = 20\log\frac{h_{te}}{200}, \qquad 30\,\text{m} < h_{te} < 1000\,\text{m} \] \[ G(h_{re}) = 10\log\frac{h_{re}}{3}, \qquad h_{re} \le 3\,\text{m} \] \[ G(h_{re}) = 20\log\frac{h_{re}}{3}, \qquad 3\,\text{m} < h_{re} < 10\,\text{m} \]
  • (\(+\)) simple, and the most accurate model available for mature cellular and land-mobile systems in cluttered urban areas.
  • (\(-\)) slow response to rapid terrain change \(\rightarrow\) good in cities, poorer in rural areas. Deviation from measurement is 10 to 14 dB.
  • (\(-\)) needs the curves, so it cannot be evaluated from formulas alone.
\(G_{\text{AREA}}\) for suburban, quasi-open and open areas.
Hata model 467
  • Hata is Okumura's curves turned into formulas, so it can be worked by hand.
  • Same measured data, so the same physical assumptions.
  • Validity conditions
    • Frequency 150 MHz to 1500 MHz.
    • Distance 1 km to 20 km.
    • BS antenna 30 m to 200 m, MS antenna 1 m to 10 m.
    • No path-specific correction is possible, unlike Okumura.
  • Urban median path loss: \[\begin{aligned} L_{50}(\text{urban}) \;=\; & 69.55 + 26.16\log f_c - 13.82\log h_{te} \\ & - a(h_{re}) + \left(44.9 - 6.55\log h_{te}\right)\log d \end{aligned}\] with \(f_c\) in MHz, \(h_{te}, h_{re}\) in m, \(d\) in km.
Okumura Vs Hata (81 Bh asks exactly this, 4)
  • Form: Okumura is graphical, Hata is closed-form.
  • Frequency: Okumura to 1920 MHz, Hata to 1500 MHz.
  • Distance: Okumura 1 to 100 km, Hata 1 to 20 km.
  • BS height: Okumura 30 to 1000 m, Hata 30 to 200 m.
  • Path-specific corrections: Okumura ✓, Hata ×
  • Accuracy: within 1 dB of Okumura for \(d > 1\) km, so Hata is preferred for large-cell work. Okumura is better for small cells and irregular terrain.
  • Extension: COST-231 extends Hata to 2 GHz by changing the constants, for PCS bands. verified/added
  • Mobile antenna correction \(a(h_{re})\):
    • small / medium city: \(\;(1.1\log f_c - 0.7)h_{re} - (1.56\log f_c - 0.8)\) dB
    • large city, \(f_c \le 300\) MHz: \(\;8.29(\log 1.54 h_{re})^2 - 1.1\) dB
    • large city, \(f_c > 300\) MHz: \(\;3.2(\log 11.75 h_{re})^2 - 4.97\) dB
  • Suburban: \(\;L_{50}(\text{urban}) - 2\left[\log(f_c/28)\right]^2 - 5.4\)
  • Open rural: \(\;L_{50}(\text{urban}) - 4.78(\log f_c)^2 + 18.33\log f_c - 40.98\)
  • Suburban and rural terms are just reductions in fixed loss for less cluttered environments.
Longley–Rice (ITS irregular terrain model)
  • Point-to-point, 40 MHz to 100 GHz, over irregular terrain.
  • Runs as a computer program. Inputs: frequency, path length, polarisation, antenna heights, surface refractivity, ground conductivity and permittivity, climate.
  • Two modes:
    • point-to-point, using a detailed terrain profile,
    • area, using empirical estimates where no profile exists.
  • (\(-\)) ignores multipath, buildings and foliage, so it is a terrain model, not an urban model.
Walfisch–Bertoni syllabus, no PYQ yet
  • Models rooftop diffraction explicitly, so it fits dense urban areas where the BS antenna is above the rooftops.
  • Path loss is the product of three factors: \[ S = P_0 \, Q^2 \, P_1 \]
    • \(P_0\) \(=\) free space loss between isotropic antennas,
    • \(Q^2\) \(=\) reduction from the row of buildings shadowing the street,
    • \(P_1\) \(=\) loss from the final rooftop-to-street diffraction.
  • Predicts an overall \(\;\propto d^{-3.8}\) roll-off, matching urban measurement.
  • Adopted as part of COST-231.
Ericsson multiple breakpoint model (80 Bh asks by name, 2)
  • Built from measurements in a multi-floor office building.
  • Uses a uniform distribution to generate path loss between a minimum and maximum bound at each distance.
  • 4 breakpoints, each carrying an upper and lower bound on path loss.
  • Assumes 30 dB attenuation at \(d_0 = 1\) m, accurate at 900 MHz w/ unity-gain antennas.
  • Slope changes from 20 dB/decade at the first breakpoint to 60 dB/decade in the final section.
  • Its value is that it gives a deterministic limit on the range of path loss, not a single number.

column1: Okumura model
column4:
• Wholly empirical. Built from extensive drive-test measurements in and around Tokyo, 1968.
  • The single most widely used model for signal prediction in urban areas.
  • Okumura published a set of curves of median attenuation relative to free space, \(A_{mu}(f,d)\), for an urban area over quasi-smooth terrain, plus correction curves.
  • Validity conditions (the 2-mark answer)
    • Frequency 150 MHz to 1920 MHz (extrapolated to 3 GHz).
    • Distance 1 km to 100 km.
    • BS antenna height 30 m to 1000 m.
    • Quasi-smooth terrain, urban reference.
  • The formula \[ \boxed{\;L_{50}(\text{dB}) = L_F + A_{mu}(f,d) - G(h_{te}) - G(h_{re}) - G_{\text{AREA}}\;} \]
    • \(L_{50}\) \(=\) median (50th percentile) path loss,
    • \(L_F\) \(=\) free space path loss,
    • \(A_{mu}\) \(=\) median attenuation relative to free space, read off the curve,
    • \(G(h_{te}), G(h_{re})\) \(=\) antenna height gain factors,
    • \(G_{\text{AREA}}\) \(=\) gain from the environment type.
\(A_{mu}(f,d)\) over a quasi-smooth urban area, \(h_{te} = 200\) m, \(h_{re} = 3\) m.
  • Height gain factors: \[ G(h_{te}) = 20\log\frac{h_{te}}{200}, \qquad 30\,\text{m} < h_{te} < 1000\,\text{m} \] \[ G(h_{re}) = 10\log\frac{h_{re}}{3}, \qquad h_{re} \le 3\,\text{m} \] \[ G(h_{re}) = 20\log\frac{h_{re}}{3}, \qquad 3\,\text{m} < h_{re} < 10\,\text{m} \]
  • (\(+\)) simple, and the most accurate model available for mature cellular and land-mobile systems in cluttered urban areas.
  • (\(-\)) slow response to rapid terrain change \(\rightarrow\) good in cities, poorer in rural areas. Deviation from measurement is 10 to 14 dB.
  • (\(-\)) needs the curves, so it cannot be evaluated from formulas alone.
\(G_{\text{AREA}}\) for suburban, quasi-open and open areas.

column1: Explain indoor propagation models (any two). What factors influence them?
column4:
How indoor differs from outdoor (the “factors” answer)
  • Distances covered are much smaller.
  • Environment varies far more over a much smaller Tx–Rx separation.
  • Propagation is governed by the same three mechanisms, but conditions are far more variable.
  • Factors that influence it:
    • Layout of the building, room sizes, corridors.
    • Construction materials: concrete, metal, plaster, glass.
    • Building type: office, residential, factory.
    • Whether doors are open or closed.
    • Where the antenna is mounted: desk height Vs ceiling.
    • Number of floors between Tx and Rx.
    • Number of windows and whether they are tinted (metallised tint is a strong reflector).
    • Movement of people and furniture.
  • Path loss exponents indoors range from 1.6 (LOS corridor, better than free space, because of waveguiding) to 6 (obstructed).
Model 1: log-distance path loss (same form as outdoor)
\[ PL(d)\,[\text{dB}] = \overline{PL}(d_0) + 10n\log\!\left(\frac{d}{d_0}\right) + X_\sigma \]
  • \(n\) and \(\sigma\) are tabulated per building type.
  • Smaller \(\sigma\) \(\rightarrow\) better accuracy.
  • \(d_0\) is typically 1 m indoors.
Model 2: attenuation factor model
\[ \begin{gathered} PL(d)\,[\text{dB}] = \overline{PL}(d_0) + 10\,n_{SF}\log\!\left(\frac{d}{d_0}\right) \\ + \text{FAF} + \sum \text{PAF} \end{gathered} \]
  • \(n_{SF}\) \(=\) path loss exponent measured on the same floor.
  • FAF \(=\) floor attenuation factor, added once per floor penetrated.
  • PAF \(=\) partition attenuation factor, summed over the partitions crossed.
  • Standard deviation drops to about 4 dB, against 13 dB for the plain log-distance model.
Partition losses
  • Hard partitions: structural walls of a room. Fixed.
  • Soft partitions: movable dividers that do not reach the ceiling.
  • Between floors: FAF is not linear in floor count. The first floor costs the most (about 15 dB), each further floor adds only 6 to 10 dB, then it saturates.
  • Reason: signal also travels out of and back into the building via windows, so the direct path stops dominating.
Measured same-floor partition losses.
Model 3: ITU indoor path loss model verified/added
\[ L_{total}\,[\text{dB}] = 20\log(f) + N\log(d) + L_f(n) - 28 \]
  • \(f\) \(=\) frequency in MHz; \(d\) \(=\) separation in metres, \(d > 1\) m.
  • \(N\) \(=\) distance power loss coefficient (tabulated per band and building type; note it plays the role of \(10n\), so \(N \approx 30\) for an office at 1.8 GHz).
  • \(L_f(n)\) \(=\) floor penetration loss factor for \(n\) floors crossed, read from a table rather than computed.
  • Why it looks different: the \(20\log f\) term and the \(-28\) constant are the free space reference folded in, so no separate \(\overline{PL}(d_0)\) measurement is needed. That is its selling point \(-\) it is fully empirical / tabulated, usable without a site survey.
Which two to write (the question always says “any two”)
  • Safest pair: log-distance \(+\) attenuation factor. They share a form, so one derivation covers both, and FAF/PAF is where the marks are.
  • ITU is the cheapest third model to add: one formula, three symbols, no derivation.
  • The Ericsson multiple breakpoint model is also an indoor model \(-\) it is written up in §3.5 with the outdoor set because 80 Bh asks for it by name there. Use it here if the paper wants a model that gives bounds rather than a mean. verified/added
  • Never write only the formula. Each model scores on what it adds over free space: \(n \ne 2\), then FAF/PAF, then floor tables.

column1: What is small-scale fading? Give its types and the factors that influence it
column4:
Definition
  • Small-scale fading \(=\) rapid fluctuation of the amplitude, phase and multipath delay of a radio signal over a short travel distance or short time interval.
  • Caused by interference between two or more copies of the transmitted signal that arrive at slightly different times.
  • The copies (multipath waves) add vectorially with random phases, so the sum behaves like noise.
  • Received power can change by 30 to 40 dB when the receiver moves a fraction of a wavelength.
  • Large-scale path loss can be ignored over such a short distance.
The three effects it produces
  • Rapid changes in signal strength over a small travel distance or time interval.
  • Random frequency modulation due to different Doppler shifts on different multipath components.
  • Time dispersion (echoes) caused by multipath propagation delays \(\rightarrow\) ISI.
Time dispersion Vs frequency dispersion
  • Time dispersion: received signal lasts longer than the transmitted one, because paths have different delays. Measured by delay spread.
  • Frequency dispersion: received signal is wider in frequency than the transmitted one, because paths have different Doppler shifts. Measured by Doppler spread.
  • Both distort the received signal, and they are independent of each other. That is why fading is classified twice over, once by each.
Impulse response model of the multipath channel syllabus, no PYQ yet
  • The channel is treated as a linear filter with a time-varying impulse response.
  • Feed it a unit impulse \(\delta(t)\) and the output is \[ h(t) \;=\; \sum_{n=1}^{N} A_n\, e^{-j\phi_n}\,\delta(t-\tau_n) \]
  • \(A_n\), \(\tau_n\), \(\phi_n\) \(=\) amplitude, arrival delay and phase of the \(n\)-th path.
  • Time variation comes from motion, so it is really \(h(t,\tau)\): \(\tau\) indexes the multipath delay, \(t\) indexes the mobile's position.
  • This one model generates everything else in the chapter: the PDP is \(|h(t,\tau)|^2\), and the delay-spread parameters are its moments.
Factors influencing small-scale fading (learn all 4)
  • Multipath propagation.
    • Random amplitude and phase of each component \(\rightarrow\) the sum fluctuates.
    • Also lengthens the time the baseband signal takes to arrive \(\rightarrow\) signal smearing \(\rightarrow\) ISI.
  • Speed of the mobile.
    • Relative motion causes a Doppler shift \(f_d\) on each component.
    • Different components arrive from different angles \(\rightarrow\) different shifts \(\rightarrow\) random FM.
  • Speed of surrounding objects.
    • If nearby objects move faster than the mobile, they dominate the fading.
    • If they move slower, ignore them.
  • Transmission bandwidth of the signal.
    • If signal bandwidth \(>\) channel bandwidth, the received signal is distorted, but its strength does not fade much over a local area.
    • If signal bandwidth \(<\) channel bandwidth, amplitude changes rapidly but the signal is not distorted in time.
    • A channel gives you distortion or fading, typically one or the other.
Multipath measurement techniques syllabus, no PYQ yet
  • Direct RF pulse sounding: transmit a narrow pulse, display the received power against delay on a scope. Simple, but a single pulse can be lost in a fade.
  • Spread spectrum sliding correlator: transmit a PN sequence, correlate at the receiver w/ a slightly slower clock so the correlation peak slides through the delays. Good dynamic range, rejects interference.
  • Swept frequency (frequency domain) sounding: sweep a network analyser across the band, measure \(S_{21}\), then inverse Fourier transform to get \(h(\tau)\). Needs a cabled link, so it suits indoor work only.

column1: Define Doppler shift and Doppler spread. Derive the expression for Doppler shift
column4:
Derivation (reproduce these 5 lines exactly)
  • Mobile moves at constant velocity \(v\) along a segment of length \(d\) from \(X\) to \(Y\), receiving from a distant source \(S\).
  • Source is far away \(\rightarrow\) the arrival angle \(\theta\) is the same at \(X\) and \(Y\).
  • Path length difference \[ \Delta l \;=\; d\cos\theta \;=\; v\,\Delta t\,\cos\theta \]
  • Phase change in the received signal \[ \Delta\phi \;=\; \frac{2\pi \Delta l}{\lambda} \;=\; \frac{2\pi v \Delta t}{\lambda}\cos\theta \]
  • Apparent frequency change is the rate of change of phase: \[ f_d \;=\; \frac{1}{2\pi}\cdot\frac{\Delta\phi}{\Delta t} \;\Longrightarrow\; \boxed{\;f_d \;=\; \frac{v}{\lambda}\cos\theta\;} \]
Mobile moving from \(X\) to \(Y\) at velocity \(v\); source \(S\) is far away, so \(\theta\) is unchanged.
Reading the result
  • \(\theta = 0^\circ\), moving towards the source: \(f_d = +v/\lambda\), maximum positive shift. Received frequency \(f_c + f_d\).
  • \(\theta = 180^\circ\), moving away: \(f_d = -v/\lambda\), maximum negative shift.
  • \(\theta = 90^\circ\), moving perpendicular: \(f_d = 0\), no shift at all.
  • Maximum Doppler shift \[ f_m = \frac{v}{\lambda} = \frac{v f_c}{c} \]
Doppler spread \(B_D\)
  • Measure of the spectral broadening caused by the time rate of change of the channel.
  • Defined as the maximum Doppler shift: \(B_D = f_m = v/\lambda\).
  • A pure tone at \(f_c\) comes out spread over \(f_c \pm f_m\).
  • Characterises the channel's frequency dispersiveness.
Significance of frequency dispersion (82 Bh)
  • It makes the channel time-varying, so the receiver must keep re-estimating it.
  • If \(B_D\) approaches the signal bandwidth, the channel changes within one symbol \(\rightarrow\) fast fading, and an irreducible BER floor that more transmit power cannot cure.
  • It sets how often an adaptive equalizer must retrain and how fast a carrier recovery loop must track.
  • Different multipath components have different \(f_d\), so the composite signal suffers random FM, heard as noise on an analog system.

column1: Explain the parameters of the mobile multipath channel
column4:
Power delay profile (PDP)
  • PDP \(=\) received power against excess delay, ie the intensity of the signal arriving through the multipath channel as a function of delay.
  • Obtained by averaging many impulse response measurements over a local area.
  • Every time-dispersion parameter below is a moment of the PDP.
A measured PDP w/ its mean excess delay, rms delay spread and 10 dB maximum excess delay marked. Note the \(-20\) dB noise threshold.
Time dispersion parameters
  • First arrival delay \(\tau_A\): delay of the first signal to reach the receiver, set by the shortest path. Used as the reference, so every other delay is an excess delay.
  • Mean excess delay \(=\) first moment of the PDP: \[ \bar{\tau} \;=\; \frac{\sum_k a_k^2 \tau_k}{\sum_k a_k^2} \;=\; \frac{\sum_k P(\tau_k)\,\tau_k}{\sum_k P(\tau_k)} \]
  • rms delay spread \(=\) square root of the second central moment: \[ \sigma_\tau = \sqrt{\overline{\tau^2} - (\bar{\tau})^2}, \qquad \overline{\tau^2} = \frac{\sum_k a_k^2 \tau_k^2}{\sum_k a_k^2} \]
  • Maximum excess delay (X dB) \(=\) \(\tau_X - \tau_0\), the delay over which multipath energy stays within X dB of the strongest component.
  • \(\sigma_\tau\) is the one that matters in practice, because it, not \(\tau_{\max}\), predicts ISI.
  • These values depend on the noise threshold chosen. Set the threshold too low and noise is counted as multipath, inflating every parameter.
Coherence bandwidth \(B_c\)
  • Definition: the range of frequencies over which the channel passes all spectral components with approximately equal gain and linear phase, ie over which the channel looks flat.
  • It is the frequency-domain dual of the rms delay spread. There is no exact relationship, only rules of thumb: \[ B_c \approx \frac{1}{50\,\sigma_\tau} \quad (\text{0.9 correlation, ``90\,\%''}) \] \[ B_c \approx \frac{1}{5\,\sigma_\tau} \quad (\text{0.5 correlation, ``50\,\%''}) \]
  • Two sinusoids separated by more than \(B_c\) are affected differently by the channel.
  • Significance: compare \(B_c\) against the signal bandwidth to decide whether the channel is flat or frequency selective. That single comparison decides whether an equalizer is needed.
Coherence time \(T_c\)
  • Definition: the time over which the channel impulse response is essentially time-invariant.
  • Dual of the Doppler spread: \[ T_c \approx \frac{1}{f_m}, \qquad T_c \approx \sqrt{\frac{9}{16\pi f_m^2}} = \frac{0.423}{f_m} \] The second (geometric mean) form is the one normally used.
  • Two signals arriving more than \(T_c\) apart are affected differently.
  • Large \(T_c\) \(\rightarrow\) channel changes slowly.
  • Significance: compare \(T_c\) against the symbol period to decide whether the channel is slow or fast fading. Also sets how often the equalizer must retrain.

column1: Rayleigh fading channel Vs Ricean fading channel, with appropriate expressions
column4:
What these distributions describe
  • Not when the signal fades, but how the received envelope is statistically distributed.
  • Both apply to flat fading channels.
Rayleigh
  • Applies when all multipath components have roughly equal amplitude and there is no dominant LOS component.
  • Physically: mobile deep in an urban area, far from the BS, no line of sight.
  • The in-phase and quadrature sums are each Gaussian, so the envelope is Rayleigh: \[ p(r) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{r}{\sigma^2}\,e^{-r^2/2\sigma^2} & 0 \le r \le \infty \\[4pt] 0 & r < 0 \end{cases} \]
  • \(\sigma\) \(=\) rms value of the received voltage before envelope detection.
  • \(\sigma^2\) \(=\) time-average power before envelope detection.
  • Phase is uniformly distributed over \(0\) to \(2\pi\).
  • Key values:
    • mean \(\;r_{\text{mean}} = \sigma\sqrt{\pi/2} = 1.2533\,\sigma\)
    • median \(\;r_{\text{median}} = 1.177\,\sigma\)
    • variance \(\;\sigma_r^2 = 0.4292\,\sigma^2\)
  • Mean and median differ by only 0.55 dB, which is why the median is used in practice.
Ricean
  • Applies when there is a stationary, non-fading, dominant component, normally a LOS path, on top of the random multipath.
  • Physically: microcell, indoor pico-cell, or a mobile with clear sight of the BS.
  • The random components add onto a fixed phasor, so: \[ p(r) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{r}{\sigma^2}\,e^{-(r^2+A^2)/2\sigma^2}\, I_0\!\left(\dfrac{Ar}{\sigma^2}\right) & A \ge 0,\; r \ge 0 \\[4pt] 0 & r < 0 \end{cases} \]
  • \(A\) \(=\) peak amplitude of the dominant signal.
  • \(I_0(\cdot)\) \(=\) modified Bessel function of the first kind, zeroth order.
  • Ricean \(K\)-factor \[ K = \frac{A^2}{2\sigma^2}, \qquad K\,[\text{dB}] = 10\log\frac{A^2}{2\sigma^2} \] \(=\) ratio of deterministic power to multipath power.
  • \(A \rightarrow 0\), ie \(K \rightarrow -\infty\) dB: Ricean degenerates into Rayleigh.
  • \(K \gg 1\): the distribution tends to Gaussian about the mean, ie almost no fading.
Rayleigh envelope pdf.
\(K = -\infty\) dB is the Rayleigh case; \(K = 6\) dB shows a dominant component pulling the distribution towards Gaussian.

column1: Chapter 3 numericals — which formulas does everything come from?
column4:
This is the heaviest numerical chapter in the subject. A propagation numerical has appeared in every one of the 23 papers. Every problem below is a real PYQ, worked in full.
The formula sheet
  • Free space (Friis) \(P_r(d) = \dfrac{P_t G_t G_r \lambda^2}{(4\pi)^2 d^2 L}\),   \(\lambda = c/f\)
  • Free space path loss \(PL = 20\log\!\left(\dfrac{4\pi d}{\lambda}\right) = 32.44 + 20\log f_{\text{MHz}} + 20\log d_{\text{km}}\)
  • Power flux density \(P_d = \dfrac{P_t G_t}{4\pi d^2} = \dfrac{|E|^2}{120\pi}\),   aperture \(A_e = \dfrac{G_r\lambda^2}{4\pi}\),   \(P_r = P_d A_e\)
  • Matched receiver \(V_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{P_r R_{\text{ant}}}\), open-circuit \(V_{\text{ant}} = 2V_{\text{rms}}\)
  • Two-ray \(P_r = P_t G_t G_r \dfrac{h_t^2 h_r^2}{d^4}\), \(PL = 40\log d - 20\log h_t - 20\log h_r\) (unity gains)
  • Log-distance \(PL(d) = PL(d_0) + 10\,n\log\!\left(\dfrac{d}{d_0}\right) + X_\sigma\)
  • Okumura \(L_{50} = L_F + A_{mu} - G(h_{te}) - G(h_{re}) - G_{\text{AREA}}\), with \(G(h_{te}) = 20\log\frac{h_{te}}{200}\), \(G(h_{re}) = 10\log\frac{h_{re}}{3}\) for \(h_{re}\le 3\) m, \(20\log\frac{h_{re}}{3}\) for \(3 < h_{re} < 10\) m
  • Hata (urban) \(L_{50} = 69.55 + 26.16\log f_c - 13.82\log h_{te} - a(h_{re}) + (44.9 - 6.55\log h_{te})\log d\)
  • Delay spread \(\bar{\tau} = \dfrac{\sum P_k \tau_k}{\sum P_k}\), \(\overline{\tau^2} = \dfrac{\sum P_k \tau_k^2}{\sum P_k}\), \(\sigma_\tau = \sqrt{\overline{\tau^2} - \bar{\tau}^2}\)
  • Coherence \(B_c \approx \dfrac{1}{50\sigma_\tau}\) (90 %), \(B_c \approx \dfrac{1}{5\sigma_\tau}\) (50 %), \(f_m = \dfrac{v}{\lambda}\), \(T_c \approx \dfrac{0.423}{f_m}\)
Units discipline, the source of most lost marks: \(P\) in W for Friis, dBm only after conversion. \(d\) in metres in \(20\log(4\pi d/\lambda)\) but in km in the 32.44 form and in Hata. \(f\) in MHz in the 32.44 form and in Hata. Always write the unit beside every number.

column1: Problem 1  Free space: received power, E-field, flux density, rms voltage
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2080 Baishakh · Q3 (b) · [8]
Assume free space propagation, a receiver is located 10 km away from a 50 w transmitter. The carrier frequency is 900 MHza. antenna gain at transmitter and receiver are 1 and 2 respectively, find:
  1. The power received at the receiver
  2. The magnitude of E-field at the receiver antenna
  3. The power flux density
  4. The rms voltage applied to the receiver input.
The receiver antenna has a purely real impedance of 50 \(\Omega\) and is matched to the receiver.
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2078 Chaitra · Q3 (b) · [2+2+2+2]
Assume free space propagation, a receiver is located 10 km away from a 50W transmitter. The carrier frequency is 900 MHz, antenna gain at transmitter and receiver is 1 and 2 respectively. Find: (i) The power received at the receiver. (ii) The magnitude of the E-field at the receiver. (iii) The rms voltage applied to the receiver input. (iv) The power flux density. Same numbers, parts (iii) and (iv) swapped. “900 MHza” is the 80 Ba paper's typo.
column4:
Step 0: wavelength
\[ \lambda = \frac{c}{f} = \frac{3\times10^{8}}{900\times10^{6}} = 0.3333\ \text{m} \]
(i) Received power
  • Friis, with \(L = 1\) (no system loss stated): \[ P_r = \frac{P_t G_t G_r \lambda^2}{(4\pi)^2 d^2} = \frac{50 \times 1 \times 2 \times (0.3333)^2}{(4\pi)^2 (10^4)^2} \] \[ = \frac{50 \times 2 \times 0.11111}{157.91 \times 10^{8}} = \frac{11.111}{1.5791\times10^{10}} = 7.0362\times10^{-10}\ \text{W} \]
  • In dBm: \[ P_r = 10\log_{10}\!\left(7.0362\times10^{-10}\times10^{3}\right) = \boxed{-61.53\ \text{dBm}} \; = -91.53\ \text{dBW} \]
(iii) Power flux density (do this before the E-field, it feeds it)
\[ P_d = \frac{P_t G_t}{4\pi d^2} = \frac{50 \times 1}{4\pi (10^4)^2} = \frac{50}{1.2566\times10^{9}} = \boxed{3.9789\times10^{-8}\ \text{W/m}^2} \]
(ii) Magnitude of the E-field
  • Free space intrinsic impedance \(\eta = 120\pi = 377\ \Omega\), and \(P_d = |E|^2/\eta\): \[ |E| = \sqrt{P_d \times 377} = \sqrt{3.9789\times10^{-8} \times 377} = \sqrt{1.5\times10^{-5}} \] \[ = \boxed{3.873\times10^{-3}\ \text{V/m}} = 3.873\ \text{mV/m} \]
Cross-check: \(P_r\) from \(P_d\) and the aperture
\[ A_e = \frac{G_r\lambda^2}{4\pi} = \frac{2 \times 0.11111}{12.566} = 0.017684\ \text{m}^2 \] \[ P_r = P_d A_e = 3.9789\times10^{-8} \times 0.017684 = 7.036\times10^{-10}\ \text{W} \quad\checkmark \text{ matches (i)} \]
(iv) rms voltage at the receiver input
  • The antenna is matched to a purely real 50 \(\Omega\) load, so the power delivered is \[ P_r = \frac{V_{\text{rms}}^2}{R_{\text{ant}}} \;\Longrightarrow\; V_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{P_r R_{\text{ant}}} \] \[ = \sqrt{7.0362\times10^{-10} \times 50} = \sqrt{3.5181\times10^{-8}} \] \[ = \boxed{1.8757\times10^{-4}\ \text{V} = 187.57\ \mu\text{V}} \]
  • If the question asks for the open-circuit antenna voltage \(V_{\text{ant}}\) instead, the matched load halves it, so \[ V_{\text{ant}} = 2 V_{\text{rms}} = 375.13\ \mu\text{V} \] Read the wording: “applied to the receiver input” is \(V_{\text{rms}}\); “induced in the antenna” is \(V_{\text{ant}}\).

column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2080 Bhadra · Q2 (a) · [6]
A wireless communication transmitter has an output power of 165 watts at a carrier frequency of 325 MHz. It is connected to an antenna with a gain of 12 dBi. The receiving antenna is 15 km away and has a gain of 6 dBi. Calculate the power delivered to the receiver, considering free-space propagation. (Assume that there are no other losses or mismatches in the system.)
column4:
• Gains are in dB, so work the whole problem in dB. Converting them to linear and using Friis directly also works but is slower and more error-prone.
  • Step 1: transmit power in dBm. \[ P_t = 10\log_{10}(165 \times 10^{3}) = 10\log_{10}(1.65\times10^{5}) = 52.17\ \text{dBm} \]
  • Step 2: free space path loss. Using the km / MHz form: \[ PL = 32.44 + 20\log_{10}(325) + 20\log_{10}(15) \] \[ = 32.44 + 50.24 + 23.52 = 106.20\ \text{dB} \] Check with \(\lambda = 3\times10^8/325\times10^6 = 0.9231\) m: \(20\log(4\pi \times 15000/0.9231) = 106.20\) dB ✓
  • Step 3: link equation. \[ P_r = P_t + G_t + G_r - PL = 52.17 + 12 + 6 - 106.20 \] \[ = \boxed{-36.03\ \text{dBm}} \]
  • Step 4: convert back to watts if asked. \[ P_r = 10^{-36.03/10}\ \text{mW} = 2.4966\times10^{-4}\ \text{mW} = \boxed{249.7\ \text{nW}} \]

column1: Problem 3  Full link budget with feeder and mismatch loss
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2072 Ashwin · Q3 · [8]
A BS transmitter has a power output of 10 watts operating at a frequency of 250 MHz. The transmitter is connected by 20 m of an RF coaxial cable, which has a loss of 3-dB/100 m specification, to an antenna that has a gain of 9 dBi. The receiving antenna is 25 km away and has a gain of 4 dBi. There is negligible loss in the receiver feeder line, but the receiver is mismatched; the receiving antenna and feeder cable are designed for 50 ohm impedance. The receiver impedance loss due to mismatch is of about 0.2 dB. Calculate the power delivered to the receiver, assuming free-space propagation.
column4:
• Step 1: transmit power in dBm. \[ P_t = 10\log_{10}(10 \times 10^{3}) = 40.00\ \text{dBm} \]
  • Step 2: transmit feeder loss. \[ L_{\text{coax}} = 20\ \text{m} \times \frac{3\ \text{dB}}{100\ \text{m}} = 0.60\ \text{dB} \]
  • Step 3: free space path loss at 25 km, 250 MHz. \[ PL = 32.44 + 20\log_{10}(250) + 20\log_{10}(25) \] \[ = 32.44 + 47.96 + 27.96 = 108.36\ \text{dB} \]
  • Step 4: assemble the budget. Every gain adds, every loss subtracts.
ItemValueNote
Transmitter output\(+40.00\) dBm10 W
Transmit feeder (coax)\(-0.60\) dB20 m at 3 dB/100 m
Transmit antenna gain\(+9.00\) dB9 dBi
Free space path loss\(-108.36\) dB25 km, 250 MHz
Receive antenna gain\(+4.00\) dB4 dBi
Receive feeder loss\(-0.00\) dBstated negligible
Receiver mismatch loss\(-0.20\) dB50 \(\Omega\) system
Power at receiver\(\mathbf{-56.16}\) dBm
\[ P_r = 40.00 - 0.60 + 9.00 - 108.36 + 4.00 - 0.20 = \boxed{-56.16\ \text{dBm}} \] \[ = 10^{-56.16/10}\ \text{mW} = 2.42\times10^{-6}\ \text{mW} = \boxed{2.42\ \text{nW}} \]

column1: Problem 4  Radio coverage range from a receiver threshold
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2070 Bhadra · Q4 · [6]
Determine the radio coverage range of a base station that transmits a RF signal at 150 W, given the receiver threshold level is \(-104\) dBm. Assume that the path loss at the first meter is 15 dB in a mobile radio propagation condition. (Path loss exponent \(=\) 4)
column4:
• Step 1: transmit power in dBm. \[ P_t = 10\log_{10}(150 \times 10^{3}) = 51.76\ \text{dBm} \]
  • Step 2: maximum allowable path loss. The link works as long as \(P_r \ge -104\) dBm, so \[ PL_{\max} = P_t - P_{r,\min} = 51.76 - (-104) = 155.76\ \text{dB} \]
  • Step 3: log-distance model with \(d_0 = 1\) m. \[ PL(d) = PL(d_0) + 10\,n\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{d}{d_0}\right) = 15 + 40\log_{10}(d) \]
  • Step 4: solve for \(d\). \[ 155.76 = 15 + 40\log_{10}(d) \] \[ \log_{10}(d) = \frac{155.76 - 15}{40} = \frac{140.76}{40} = 3.519 \] \[ d = 10^{3.519} = \boxed{3304\ \text{m} \approx 3.30\ \text{km}} \]
  • Sanity check: at 3.3 km with \(n=4\) the loss beyond 1 m is \(40\log(3304) = 140.8\) dB, plus the 15 dB first-metre loss gives 155.8 dB, which is exactly the budget. ✓

column1: Problem 5  Monopole aperture and two-ray received power
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2071 Bhadra · Q4 · [6]
A mobile is located 5 km away from a base station and a vertical \(\lambda/4\) monopole antenna with a gain of 2.55 dB to receive cellular radio signals. The electric field at 1 km from the transmitter is measured to be \(10^{-3}\) V/m. The carrier frequency used for this system is 900 MHz.
  1. Find the length and effective aperture of the receiving antenna.
  2. Find the received power at the mobile using two ray ground reflection model assuming the height of the transmitting antenna is 50 m and the receiving antenna is 1.5 m above ground.
column4:
(a) Length and effective aperture
  • \[ \lambda = \frac{3\times10^{8}}{900\times10^{6}} = 0.3333\ \text{m} \]
  • Length of a quarter-wave monopole: \[ L = \frac{\lambda}{4} = \frac{0.3333}{4} = \boxed{0.0833\ \text{m} = 8.33\ \text{cm}} \]
  • Gain in linear terms: \[ G_r = 10^{2.55/10} = 1.7989 \]
  • Effective aperture: \[ A_e = \frac{G_r \lambda^2}{4\pi} = \frac{1.7989 \times 0.11111}{12.566} = \boxed{0.0159\ \text{m}^2} \]
(b) Received power from the two-ray model
  • Step 1: the two-ray E-field. For \(d\) well beyond the crossover distance, \[ |E_{\text{tot}}(d)| = \frac{2 E_0 d_0}{d} \cdot \frac{2\pi h_t h_r}{\lambda d} \] with the reference \(E_0 d_0 = 10^{-3} \times 1000 = 1\) V (measured at \(d_0 = 1\) km).
  • Step 2: substitute. \[ |E_{\text{tot}}| = \frac{2 \times 1}{5000} \cdot \frac{2\pi \times 50 \times 1.5}{0.3333 \times 5000} \] \[ = 4\times10^{-4} \times \frac{471.24}{1666.7} = 4\times10^{-4} \times 0.28274 \] \[ = \boxed{1.131\times10^{-4}\ \text{V/m}} \]
  • Step 3: convert field to power through the aperture. \[ P_r = \frac{|E_{\text{tot}}|^2}{120\pi} \cdot A_e = \frac{(1.131\times10^{-4})^2}{377} \times 0.0159 \] \[ = \frac{1.2791\times10^{-8}}{377} \times 0.0159 = 3.3928\times10^{-11} \times 0.0159 \] \[ = \boxed{5.397\times10^{-13}\ \text{W} = -92.68\ \text{dBm}} \]
  • Check the model is valid here: crossover distance \(d_c = 4\pi h_t h_r/\lambda = 4\pi(50)(1.5)/0.3333 = 2827\) m. Since \(d = 5000\ \text{m} > d_c\), the \(1/d^2\) field approximation holds. ✓

column1: Problem 6  Free space path loss of a cordless phone
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2077 Chaitra · Q3 · [6]
Given a cordless phone operating at 52000 kHz frequency which has a range of 50m. Determine the free space path loss.
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2080 Chaitra · Q4 (b) · [2+4]
Define Doppler's effect in Small Scale Fading. (i) Given a cordless phone operating at 52000 kHz frequency which has a range of 50m. Determine the free space path loss.
column4:
• Step 1: sort out the units. \[ f = 52000\ \text{kHz} = 52\ \text{MHz} = 52\times10^{6}\ \text{Hz} \] The “52000 kHz” is deliberately awkward. Convert it first.
  • Step 2: wavelength. \[ \lambda = \frac{3\times10^{8}}{52\times10^{6}} = 5.769\ \text{m} \]
  • Step 3: path loss. \[ PL = 20\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{4\pi d}{\lambda}\right) = 20\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{4\pi \times 50}{5.769}\right) \] \[ = 20\log_{10}(108.9) = \boxed{40.74\ \text{dB}} \]
  • Cross-check with the km / MHz form, \(d = 0.05\) km: \[ PL = 32.44 + 20\log(52) + 20\log(0.05) = 32.44 + 34.32 - 26.02 = 40.74\ \text{dB} \quad\checkmark \]
  • Note how low this is compared with the 100 dB-plus figures elsewhere: short range and a long wavelength both help. That is why cordless phones need only milliwatts.

column1: Problem 7  dBm, dBW and received power at two distances
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2081 Baishakh · Q3 (b) · [1+1+2+2]
If a transmitter produces 50 watts of power, express the transmit power in units of (i) dBm, and (ii) dBW. If 50 watts is applied to a unity gain antenna with a 900 MHz carrier frequency, find the received power in dBm at a free space distance of 100 m from the antenna. What is \(P_r\) (10 km)? Assume unity gain for the receiver antenna.
column4:
• (i) \[ P_t\,[\text{dBm}] = 10\log_{10}(50 \times 10^{3}) = 10\log_{10}(5\times10^{4}) = \boxed{46.99\ \text{dBm}} \]
  • (ii) \[ P_t\,[\text{dBW}] = 10\log_{10}(50) = \boxed{16.99\ \text{dBW}} \] Always \(\text{dBm} = \text{dBW} + 30\). ✓
  • (iii) At \(d = 100\) m, \(\lambda = 0.3333\) m, \(G_t = G_r = 1\): \[ P_r = \frac{50 \times 1 \times 1 \times (0.3333)^2}{(4\pi)^2 (100)^2} = \frac{5.5556}{157.91 \times 10^{4}} = 3.5181\times10^{-6}\ \text{W} \] \[ = 10\log_{10}(3.5181\times10^{-3}\ \text{mW}) = \boxed{-24.54\ \text{dBm}} \]
  • (iv) At \(d = 10\) km, use the \(1/d^2\) scaling instead of recomputing: \[ P_r(10\ \text{km}) = P_r(100\ \text{m}) \left(\frac{100}{10000}\right)^{2} = 3.5181\times10^{-6} \times 10^{-4} \] \[ = 3.5181\times10^{-10}\ \text{W} = \boxed{-64.54\ \text{dBm}} \]
  • The shortcut in dB: the distance grew by a factor 100, ie 2 decades, and free space costs 20 dB per decade, so \(-24.54 - 40 = -64.54\) dBm. ✓

column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2079 Chaitra · Q4 (b) · [3+3]
Explain basic propagation models. Compute the far field distance for an antenna with maximum dimension of 1 m and operating frequency of 900 MHz.
column4:
• \[ \lambda = \frac{3\times10^{8}}{900\times10^{6}} = 0.3333\ \text{m} \]
  • \[ d_f = \frac{2D^2}{\lambda} = \frac{2 \times (1)^2}{0.3333} = \boxed{6\ \text{m}} \]
  • Verify both side conditions:
    • \(d_f \gg D\): \(6 \gg 1\) ✓
    • \(d_f \gg \lambda\): \(6 \gg 0.3333\) ✓

column1: Problem 9  Okumura model: median path loss and received power
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2080 Bhadra · Q3 (b) · [4+2+2]
Determine the mean path loss using Okumura's model for \(d = 50\) km, \(h_{te} = 100\) m, \(h_{re} = 10\) m in a suburban environment. If the base station transmitter radiates an EIRP of 1kW at a carrier frequency of 900 MHz. Find EIRP (dBm) and the power at the receiver where the gain at receiving antenna is 10 dB. The medium attenuation factor is 43 dB and the gain due to area is 9 dB for a 50 km distance and 900 MHz frequency of operation.
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2082 Bhadra · Q3 (b) · [5]
Find the mean path loss using Okumura's Model for \(d = 50\) km, \(h_{te} = 100\)m, \(h_{re} = 10\)m in a suburban environment. If the BS transmitter radiates an EIRP oh 1 kW at a carrier frequency of 900 MHz, find EIRP in dBm and the power at the receiver where gain of receiving antenna is 10 dB. (Given: \(A_{mu}(f,d) = 43\) dB, \(G_{Area}(f) = 9\) dB)
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2074 Magh · Q3 · [4+4]
Explain Okumura model of outdoor radio propagation. Determine the median path loss for T-R separation of 50Km, transmit antenna effective height of 100m and receive antenna effective height of 10m in a suburban area with correction factor of 9dB at 900MHz. Assume median attenuation relative to free space 43dB.
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2082 Baishakh · Q4 · [8]
Find the median path loss sing Okumura's model for \(d = 50\) km, \(h_{te} = 100\) m, \(h_{re} = 10\) m in a suburban environment. If the base station transmitter radiates an EIRP of 1 kW at a carrier frequency of 900 MHz, find the power at the receiver (assume a unity gain receiving antenna). [Assume \(A_{mu} = 43\) dB, \(G_{AREA} = 9\) dB]
column4:
One set of numbers, four papers. “EIRP oh 1 kW” is the 82 Bh paper's own typo, and “path loss sing” is 82 Ba's. 82 Ba is the only one with a unity-gain receiver, and it does not ask for EIRP in dBm — see Step 4.
Step 1: free space path loss at 50 km, 900 MHz
\[ \lambda = 0.3333\ \text{m} \] \[ L_F = 20\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{4\pi \times 50\times10^{3}}{0.3333}\right) = 20\log_{10}(1.885\times10^{6}) = 125.51\ \text{dB} \] Check: \(32.44 + 20\log(900) + 20\log(50) = 32.44 + 59.08 + 33.98 = 125.50\) dB ✓
Step 2: antenna height gain factors
  • Base station, \(h_{te} = 100\) m (valid, since \(30 < 100 < 1000\) m): \[ G(h_{te}) = 20\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{100}{200}\right) = 20\log_{10}(0.5) = -6.02\ \text{dB} \] Negative, because 100 m is below the 200 m reference.
  • Mobile, \(h_{re} = 10\) m. Since \(3 < h_{re} < 10\) m the 20 log branch applies: \[ G(h_{re}) = 20\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{10}{3}\right) = 20\log_{10}(3.333) = +10.46\ \text{dB} \] Choosing the wrong branch here is the standard error. Check \(h_{re}\) against 3 m first.
Step 3: assemble the Okumura result
\[ L_{50} = L_F + A_{mu} - G(h_{te}) - G(h_{re}) - G_{\text{AREA}} \] \[ = 125.51 + 43 - (-6.02) - (10.46) - 9 \] \[ = 125.51 + 43 + 6.02 - 10.46 - 9 = \boxed{155.07\ \text{dB}} \]
Step 4 (80 Bh, 82 Bh): EIRP and received power
  • \[ \text{EIRP} = 1\ \text{kW} = 1000\ \text{W} \;\Rightarrow\; 10\log_{10}(1000 \times 10^{3}) = \boxed{60\ \text{dBm}} \]
  • \[ P_r = \text{EIRP} - L_{50} + G_r = 60 - 155.07 + 10 = \boxed{-85.07\ \text{dBm}} \]
  • \[ = 10^{-85.07/10}\ \text{mW} = 3.11\times10^{-9}\ \text{mW} = 3.11\ \text{pW} \]
  • Interpretation: \(-85\) dBm is a usable but not comfortable level. Typical GSM sensitivity is around \(-104\) dBm, so this link has about 19 dB of margin.
  • 82 Ba variant — unity gain receiver. That paper asks only for \(P_r\), with \(G_r = 1\), ie 0 dB: \[ P_r = 60 - 155.07 + 0 = \boxed{-95.07\ \text{dBm}} = 0.311\ \text{pW} \] Exactly 10 dB below the 80 Bh / 82 Bh answer, since the only change is dropping the 10 dB receive gain. Margin over \(-104\) dBm falls to about 9 dB.

column1: Problem 10  Okumura run backwards: find the T–R separation
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2077 Chaitra · Q4 (b) · [8]
Employing the Okumura model compute the transmitter and receiver separation distance if median loss is 167 dB when the carrier frequency is 2.1 GHz. Assume height of transmitting antenna is 40 m, height of receiving antenna is 2 m, for a large city. [\(A_{mu} = 34\) dB, \(G_{area} = 0\) dB]
column4:
• Step 1: the height gain factors. \[ G(h_{te}) = 20\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{40}{200}\right) = 20\log_{10}(0.2) = -13.98\ \text{dB} \] \[ h_{re} = 2\ \text{m} \le 3\ \text{m} \;\Rightarrow\; G(h_{re}) = 10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{2}{3}\right) = -1.76\ \text{dB} \] Here the 10 log branch applies. Compare with Problem 9, where it was 20 log.
  • Step 2: rearrange Okumura for \(L_F\). \[ L_{50} = L_F + A_{mu} - G(h_{te}) - G(h_{re}) - G_{\text{area}} \] \[ L_F = L_{50} - A_{mu} + G(h_{te}) + G(h_{re}) + G_{\text{area}} \] \[ = 167 - 34 + (-13.98) + (-1.76) + 0 = \boxed{117.26\ \text{dB}} \]
  • Step 3: invert the free space formula. \[ \lambda = \frac{3\times10^{8}}{2.1\times10^{9}} = 0.1429\ \text{m} \] \[ L_F = 20\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{4\pi d}{\lambda}\right) \;\Longrightarrow\; d = \frac{\lambda}{4\pi}\,10^{L_F/20} \] \[ = \frac{0.1429}{12.566} \times 10^{117.26/20} = 0.011370 \times 10^{5.863} \] \[ = 0.011370 \times 7.2934\times10^{5} = \boxed{8292\ \text{m} \approx 8.29\ \text{km}} \]
  • Sanity check: substituting \(d = 8.29\) km back gives \(L_F = 32.44 + 20\log(2100) + 20\log(8.292) = 32.44 + 66.44 + 18.38 = 117.26\) dB ✓

column1: Problem 11  Hata model, and comparison with free space

QUESTION AS PRINTED 2079 Bhadra · Q3 (b) · [4+4]

column1: Problem 12  Hata run backwards: maximum cell radius and area
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2073 Magh · Q3 (b) · [6]
Let us consider a medium sized city and assume the typical GSM downlink parameters. The Base Station (BS) is transmitting with power 50W. The minimum acceptable received power at Mobile Station (MS) is \(-91\) dBm. The carrier frequency is 900 MHz, the height of BS is 30m and height of MS is 1m. Estimate the maximum cell radius and corresponding cell area using Hata Model. The paper prints the full Hata model box in its header: \(L_{50}\)(urban) \(= 69.55 + 26.16\log f_c - 13.82\log h_{te} - a(h_{re}) + (44.9 - 6.55\log h_{te})\log d\), with \(a(h_{re}) = (1.1\log f_c - 0.7)h_{re} - (1.56\log f_c - 0.8)\) dB for a medium sized city.
column4:
• Step 1: allowable path loss. \[ P_t = 10\log_{10}(50\times10^{3}) = 46.99\ \text{dBm} \] \[ PL_{\max} = 46.99 - (-91) = 137.99\ \text{dB} \]
  • Step 2: correction factor, medium city, \(\log_{10}(900) = 2.9542\): \[ a(h_{re}) = (1.1 \times 2.9542 - 0.7)(1) - (1.56 \times 2.9542 - 0.8) \] \[ = (3.2496 - 0.7) - (4.6086 - 0.8) = 2.5496 - 3.8086 = \boxed{-1.259\ \text{dB}} \] A negative correction is normal for a 1 m mobile antenna.
  • Step 3: split Hata into \(L_{50} = A + B\log d\). With \(\log_{10}(30) = 1.4771\): \[ A = 69.55 + 26.16(2.9542) - 13.82(1.4771) - (-1.259) \] \[ = 69.55 + 77.281 - 20.413 + 1.259 = 127.678 \] \[ B = 44.9 - 6.55(1.4771) = 44.9 - 9.675 = 35.225 \]
  • Step 4: solve for \(d\). \[ 137.99 = 127.678 + 35.225\log_{10} d \] \[ \log_{10} d = \frac{137.99 - 127.678}{35.225} = \frac{10.312}{35.225} = 0.29274 \] \[ d = 10^{0.29274} = \boxed{1.962\ \text{km}} \]
  • Step 5: cell area. Treating the cell as a regular hexagon of radius \(R = d\): \[ A_{\text{cell}} = 2.598\,R^2 = 2.598 \times (1.962)^2 = 2.598 \times 3.850 = \boxed{10.00\ \text{km}^2} \] If the cell is taken as a circle instead, \(\pi R^2 = 12.10\) km\(^2\). State which you used.
  • Note \(d = 1.96\) km is just below the Hata validity floor of 1 km, so the answer sits at the edge of the model's range. Mention this: it is worth a mark.

column1: Problem 14  Two-ray Vs free space path loss
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2070 Magh · Q3 · [4+4]
Determine the propagation path loss for signal at 800 MHZ, with a transmitting antenna height of 30 m and a receiving antenna height of 2 m, over a distance of 10 km, using two-ray mobile point-to-point propagation model. How is it compared with that of free-space propagation path loss model?
column4:
• Step 1: check the model is valid. \[ \lambda = \frac{3\times10^{8}}{800\times10^{6}} = 0.375\ \text{m} \] \[ d_c = \frac{4\pi h_t h_r}{\lambda} = \frac{4\pi \times 30 \times 2}{0.375} = \frac{754.0}{0.375} = 2011\ \text{m} = 2.01\ \text{km} \] Since \(d = 10\ \text{km} > d_c\), the \(d^{-4}\) form applies. ✓ Always do this check first: below \(d_c\) the two-ray model oscillates and this formula is wrong.
  • Step 2: two-ray path loss (unity antenna gains): \[ PL = 40\log_{10} d - \left(20\log_{10} h_t + 20\log_{10} h_r\right) \] \[ = 40\log_{10}(10\,000) - 20\log_{10}(30) - 20\log_{10}(2) \] \[ = 40(4) - 29.54 - 6.02 = 160 - 35.56 = \boxed{124.44\ \text{dB}} \]
  • Step 3: free space path loss at the same distance. \[ PL_{FS} = 32.44 + 20\log(800) + 20\log(10) = 32.44 + 58.06 + 20 = \boxed{110.50\ \text{dB}} \]
  • Step 4: comparison. \[ PL_{2\text{-ray}} - PL_{FS} = 124.44 - 110.50 = \boxed{13.94\ \text{dB} \text{ worse}} \]
  • Why the two-ray model predicts more loss: the ground-reflected ray arrives almost exactly out of phase with the direct ray and partially cancels it. Free space ignores that ray entirely, so it is over-optimistic.
  • Note also: the two-ray answer contains no \(\lambda\) term, so it is frequency independent, while the free space answer is not.

column1: Problem 16  Feasibility of a 10 km link at 2.4 GHz
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2074 Bhadra · Q3 · [12]
Estimate the feasibility of a 10-km wireless link in suburban area, with one access point and one client radio, using Okumura model for path loss. The median attenuation value is 20 dB and gain due to environment is 13 dB. The height of access point antenna is 100 m and that of client antennal is 10 m:
  1. Access point is connected to antenna with 5-dBi gain, with a transmitting power of 20-dBm and a receive sensitivity of \(-80\)-dBm
  2. Client is connected to antenna with 20-dBi gain, with a transmitting power of 15-dBm and a receive sensitivity of \(-75\)-dBm
  3. Cables in both systems are short, with a loss of 3-dB at each side at 2.4-GHz frequency of operation.
column4:
• Step 1: free space loss at 10 km, 2.4 GHz. \[ \lambda = \frac{3\times10^{8}}{2.4\times10^{9}} = 0.125\ \text{m} \] \[ L_F = 32.44 + 20\log(2400) + 20\log(10) = 32.44 + 67.60 + 20 = 120.05\ \text{dB} \]
  • Step 2: Okumura median path loss. \[ G(h_{te}) = 20\log(100/200) = -6.02\ \text{dB}, \qquad G(h_{re}) = 20\log(10/3) = +10.46\ \text{dB} \] \[ L_{50} = 120.05 + 20 - (-6.02) - 10.46 - 13 = \boxed{122.61\ \text{dB}} \]
  • Step 3: forward link, AP \(\rightarrow\) client. \[ P_r = 20 + 5 - 3 + 20 - 3 - 122.61 = -83.61\ \text{dBm} \] Client sensitivity is \(-75\) dBm, so the margin is \[ -83.61 - (-75) = \boxed{-8.61\ \text{dB}} \quad \text{(shortfall)} \]
  • Step 4: reverse link, client \(\rightarrow\) AP. \[ P_r = 15 + 20 - 3 + 5 - 3 - 122.61 = -88.61\ \text{dBm} \] AP sensitivity is \(-80\) dBm, so the margin is \[ -88.61 - (-80) = \boxed{-8.61\ \text{dB}} \quad \text{(shortfall)} \]
  • Step 5: verdict. Both directions fall 8.6 dB short, so the 10 km link is NOT feasible as specified, and it fails symmetrically, so no single end can be blamed.
  • Step 6: what distance would work? Set the margin to zero: \[ L_{50,\max} = 122.61 - 8.61 = 114.00\ \text{dB} \] \[ L_F = 114.00 - 20 + (-6.02) + 10.46 + 13 = 111.44\ \text{dB} \] \[ d = \frac{0.125}{12.566}\,10^{111.44/20} = 0.009947 \times 3.729\times10^{5} = \boxed{3.71\ \text{km}} \]
  • How to fix it (worth stating): raise the antenna gains, raise the AP height (each doubling of \(h_{te}\) buys 6 dB), or accept a shorter link. Raising transmit power by 8.6 dB would also do it but may breach the licence-exempt limit at 2.4 GHz.

column1: Problem 17  Power delay profile: delay spread and coherence bandwidth
column4:
The method, once
  • Step 1: convert every dB power to a linear ratio, \(P_k = 10^{(\text{dB})/10}\). Never average in dB.
  • Step 2: mean excess delay \(\;\bar{\tau} = \dfrac{\sum P_k\tau_k}{\sum P_k}\)
  • Step 3: second moment \(\;\overline{\tau^2} = \dfrac{\sum P_k\tau_k^2}{\sum P_k}\)
  • Step 4: rms delay spread \(\;\sigma_\tau = \sqrt{\overline{\tau^2} - \bar{\tau}^2}\)
  • Step 5: coherence bandwidth \(\;B_c = \dfrac{1}{50\sigma_\tau}\) (90 %) or \(\dfrac{1}{5\sigma_\tau}\) (50 %).

  • \[ B_c(50\%) = \frac{1}{5 \times 1.375} = \boxed{0.1455\ \text{Hz}} \]
  • Source defect, state it: the paper prints the delays in seconds. A real multipath channel has delays of microseconds, and a 0.15 Hz coherence bandwidth is physically impossible. Solve it as printed, then add one line noting that with \(\mu\)s the answers become \(\bar{\tau} = 4.38\ \mu\)s, \(\sigma_\tau = 1.375\ \mu\)s, \(B_c(50\%) = 145.5\) kHz.

column1: Problem 18  Doppler shift and coherence time
column3:
PROBLEM not a PYQ · the standard Rappaport example verified/added
A US digital cellular system operating at \(f_c = 900\) MHz serves a vehicle moving at 70 km/h. Compute the received carrier frequency when the mobile moves (a) directly towards the transmitter, (b) directly away from it, and (c) perpendicular to the direction of arrival. Hence find the Doppler spread and the 50% coherence time.
column4:
Four papers ask for the Doppler derivation in prose (78 Ch, 81 Ba, 80 Ch, 82 Bh) and none prints numbers. This worked example is what turns that derivation into a full answer. verified/added
  • Step 1: convert the velocity. Always to m/s. \[ v = 70\ \frac{\text{km}}{\text{h}} \times \frac{1000}{3600} = 19.444\ \text{m/s} \]
  • Step 2: wavelength and maximum Doppler shift. \[ \lambda = \frac{3\times10^{8}}{900\times10^{6}} = 0.3333\ \text{m} \] \[ f_m = \frac{v}{\lambda} = \frac{19.444}{0.3333} = \boxed{58.33\ \text{Hz}} \]
  • (a) Towards the transmitter, \(\theta = 0^\circ\), \(\cos\theta = +1\): \[ f_d = +58.33\ \text{Hz} \;\Rightarrow\; f = 900\ \text{MHz} + 58.33\ \text{Hz} = \boxed{900.00005833\ \text{MHz}} \]
  • (b) Away, \(\theta = 180^\circ\), \(\cos\theta = -1\): \[ f_d = -58.33\ \text{Hz} \;\Rightarrow\; f = \boxed{899.99994167\ \text{MHz}} \]
  • (c) Perpendicular, \(\theta = 90^\circ\), \(\cos\theta = 0\): \[ f_d = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; f = \boxed{900\ \text{MHz exactly}} \]
  • Step 3: coherence time. \[ T_c \approx \frac{0.423}{f_m} = \frac{0.423}{58.33} = 7.25\ \text{ms} \]
  • Interpretation: the channel stays essentially constant for only 7.25 ms. A GSM burst is 0.577 ms, so the channel is safely static within one burst, which is exactly the design intent. A data frame lasting longer than 7 ms would see the channel change under it.

column1: Advantages of digital modulation over analog
column4:
Modulation itself
  • Process of impressing message on high-freq carrier suitable for transmission.
  • Translates baseband (modulating) signal \(\rightarrow\) bandpass (modulated) signal.
  • Why: antenna size \(\propto \lambda\), so baseband speech at 3 kHz needs km-long antennas.
  • Why: shifting to different carriers lets many users share one medium (multiple access).
  • Why: higher freq \(\rightarrow\) longer range, smaller hardware.
Digital over analog 2
  • Regenerable: noise does not accumulate, receiver rebuilds clean symbols.
  • Resistant to fading, noise, interference.
  • Voice \(+\) data \(+\) video multiplexed on one channel.
  • Encryption possible \(\rightarrow\) security and privacy.
  • Error control coding detects and corrects errors (Ch 6).
  • Built in DSP software, not analog hardware \(\rightarrow\) cheap, small, reprogrammable.
  • Equalization and diversity apply cleanly (Ch 5).
  • Cost: needs more bandwidth per message and needs synchronisation.
Power efficiency \(\eta_p\)
  • Ability to hold message quality at low power (low SNR).
  • \(\eta_p = E_b/N_0\) at a stated BER, usually \(10^{-5}\).
  • \(E_b =\) energy per bit, \(N_0 =\) noise power spectral density.
  • Trade-off: BER \(\uparrow\) as \(E_b/N_0 \downarrow\).
  • Lower \(E_b/N_0\) for the same BER \(=\) more power efficient.
Bandwidth efficiency \(\eta_B\)
  • Ability to carry data in a limited band.
  • \(\eta_B = R/B\) bps/Hz, \(R =\) data rate, \(B =\) RF bandwidth.
  • Ceiling set by Shannon: \(\eta_{B(\max)} = C/B = \log_2(1 + S/N)\).
  • The fundamental trade-off: improve \(\eta_p\) and \(\eta_B\) gets worse, and the reverse. No scheme wins both.
  • M-ary buys \(\eta_B\) by spending \(\eta_p\).
Choosing a scheme for a mobile link
  • Low BER at low SNR (handset battery is finite).
  • Resistance to interference (ACI, CCI) and multipath fading.
  • Minimum occupied bandwidth (spectrum is bought, not free).
  • Cheap, small, low-power to implement in the handset.
  • No scheme meets all four, so every standard is a trade-off.
Constellation (signal space) diagram
  • Graphical plot of the complex envelope of every possible symbol.
  • \(x\) axis \(=\) in-phase component, \(y\) axis \(=\) quadrature component.
  • Distance of a point from origin \(=\) amplitude, so distance\(^2\) \(=\) symbol power.
  • Distance \(d\) between the two nearest points sets noise immunity.
  • \(P_e \propto Q\!\left(\dfrac{d}{\sqrt{2N_0}}\right)\), so small \(d\) \(\rightarrow\) high BER.
  • Farthest point from origin \(=\) peak power the amplifier must deliver.
The three binary keying waveforms against one data stream: (a) ASK, (b) BFSK, (c) BPSK. SST, Modulation extra note

column1: QPSK: transmission and detection process +Fig, constellation diagram
column4:
Idea
  • M-ary PSK with \(M = 4\), so 2 bits per symbol (a dibit).
  • Carrier phase takes one of 4 equally spaced values \(\pi/4,\, 3\pi/4,\, 5\pi/4,\, 7\pi/4\).
  • \(s_i(t) = \sqrt{\dfrac{2E_s}{T_s}}\cos\!\big(2\pi f_c t + (2i-1)\tfrac{\pi}{4}\big)\), \(i = 1,2,3,4\).
  • Symbol period \(T_s = 2T_b\) \(\rightarrow\) half the bandwidth of BPSK for the same bit rate.
  • Null-to-null RF bandwidth \(= R_b\) (BPSK needs \(2R_b\)), so \(\eta_B = 1\) bps/Hz.
  • BER identical to BPSK: the dibit splits into two independent BPSK streams on orthogonal carriers, \(P_e = Q\!\left(\sqrt{2E_b/N_0}\right)\).
  • So QPSK gets double the bandwidth efficiency for free. That is the whole selling point.
  • Symbols are Gray coded (00, 01, 11, 10 around the circle) so a wrong symbol costs only 1 bit.
QPSK constellation: 4 points, one per dibit, spaced \(90^\circ\). Distance to origin \(= \sqrt{E_s}\), distance between neighbours \(= \sqrt{2E_s} = 2\sqrt{E_b}\). SST, Modulation extra note
QPSK transmitter. SST, Fig 3.2.3
Transmission process 4
  1. Binary stream at \(f_b\) bps enters a bipolar NRZ encoder \(\rightarrow\) \(\pm 1\) levels.
  2. Serial-to-parallel converter splits it: even-numbered bits \(\rightarrow\) \(I(t)\), odd-numbered bits \(\rightarrow\) \(Q(t)\), each at \(f_b/2\) bps.
  3. \(I(t)\) multiplied by \(\cos 2\pi f_c t\) in balance modulator 1.
  4. \(Q(t)\) multiplied by \(\sin 2\pi f_c t\) (carrier through a \(90^\circ\) shifter) in balance modulator 2.
  5. Summer adds the two \(\rightarrow\) QPSK signal, one of 4 phases per dibit.
  6. Output BPF limits the spectrum to the allocated channel.
QPSK receiver, a pair of coherent correlators. SST, Modulation extra note
Detection process 4
  1. Received QPSK splits into two arms (coherent detection, so carrier recovery circuit supplies \(\cos\) and \(\sin\) references).
  2. Upper arm: product modulator with \(\cos 2\pi f_c t\), then integrate-and-dump over \(0\) to \(T_b\) \(\rightarrow\) output \(x_1\).
  3. Lower arm: product modulator with \(\sin 2\pi f_c t\), then integrator \(\rightarrow\) output \(x_2\).
  4. Decision device, threshold \(0\) V: \(x_1 > 0 \rightarrow\) 1, \(x_1 < 0 \rightarrow\) 0 on the I channel, same rule for \(x_2\) on the Q channel.
  5. Multiplexer interleaves the two recovered streams \(\rightarrow\) original binary sequence.
Say “coherent” out loud. QPSK cannot be envelope detected, the receiver needs the carrier phase.
The weakness that produced OQPSK and \(\pi/4\)-QPSK
  • When both bits of a dibit change, the phase jumps \(180^\circ\) and the envelope passes through zero.
  • After the transmitter's band-limiting filter this zero crossing becomes a deep amplitude dip.
  • A non-linear (efficient) amplifier hard-limits that dip \(\rightarrow\) the filtered sidelobes grow back \(\rightarrow\) adjacent channel interference returns.
  • Fixing this without giving up bandwidth efficiency is the whole story of §4.3 and §4.4.

column1: DPSK modulation: transmitter and receiver; PN sequence and why it is used
column4:
What DPSK is
  • Non-coherent form of PSK: no synchronous carrier needed at the receiver.
  • Information sits in the difference between the phases of two successive symbols, not in the absolute phase.
  • Encoding rule: symbol 1 \(=\) no phase transition, symbol 0 \(=\) \(180^\circ\) transition.
  • So the present bit is decoded by comparing against the previous bit.
  • \(P_{e} = \tfrac{1}{2}e^{-E_b/N_0}\), about 3 dB worse than coherent BPSK at high SNR.
Transmitter 2
  1. Binary sequence \(m_k\) enters a logic (differential encoder) circuit.
  2. A 1-bit delay \(T_b\) feeds the previous encoded bit \(d_{k-1}\) back to it.
  3. Encoder output \(d_k\) toggles when \(m_k = 0\) and holds when \(m_k = 1\).
  4. Bipolar NRZ encoder \(\rightarrow\) \(\pm 1\) levels.
  5. Balance modulator multiplies by the carrier \(\rightarrow\) DPSK out.
DPSK transmitter: encoder \(+\) \(T_b\) delay ahead of an ordinary BPSK modulator. SST, Modulation extra note
DPSK receiver: the signal is its own phase reference. SST, Modulation extra note
Receiver 2
  1. Bandpass filter centred on \(f_c\) removes out-of-band noise.
  2. Signal is multiplied by its own \(T_b\)-delayed copy in the correlator.
  3. Integrate and dump over one bit gives an output proportional to \(\cos\phi\), where \(\phi\) is the phase difference between the two.
  4. \(\phi = 0 \rightarrow\) output positive \(\rightarrow\) decide 1.
    \(\phi = \pi \rightarrow\) output negative \(\rightarrow\) decide 0.
  5. Decision device at threshold \(\lambda = 0\) V rebuilds the sequence.
No carrier recovery circuit anywhere in this diagram. That is the mark the examiner is looking for.
Differential encoding worked through: the starred bit is the arbitrary reference. Row 2 is \(d_k\), row 3 its phase, last row the recovered data. SST, Modulation extra note
DPSK against BPSK
  • Bandwidth \(f_b\) against \(2 f_b\) \(\rightarrow\) DPSK halves it.
  • Carrier at demodulator: not required against required.
  • Error probability: higher against low.
  • Bit detection: over two successive bit intervals against a single interval.
  • Circuit: simpler receiver, but the encoder adds transmitter complexity.
(+) and (-)
  • (+) No carrier recovery \(\rightarrow\) cheap, small, fast to acquire.
  • (+) Works where the channel rotates phase faster than a PLL can track.
  • (-) \(P_e\) roughly 3 dB worse than coherent BPSK.
  • (-) Errors propagate in pairs: one bad symbol corrupts the reference for the next.
PN sequence and why it is used 2+2 (full treatment in §4.7)
  • PN (pseudo-noise) sequence \(=\) a coded sequence of 1s and 0s that looks random to anyone without the generator, but is completely deterministic and repeatable.
  • Generated by an \(m\)-stage shift register with XOR (parity) feedback; maximal-length period \(= 2^m - 1\) chips.
  • Properties: 1s and 0s roughly equiprobable; sharp autocorrelation peak and near-zero elsewhere; low cross-correlation between different codes; adding a shifted copy gives the same sequence in a new phase; easy to generate and synchronise.
  • Why used: spreads the spectrum, so the signal hides under the noise floor (low probability of intercept) and shrugs off narrowband jamming.
  • Why used: nearly orthogonal codes let many users share one band at once \(\rightarrow\) CDMA.
  • Why used: gives the receiver a unique pattern to correlate against, which is both the addressing scheme and the synchronisation reference.

column1: OQPSK transmitter and receiver; why \(\pi/4\)-QPSK is preferred over OQPSK
column4:
Offset QPSK (OQPSK), also called staggered QPSK
  • Same circuit as QPSK, with one change: the \(Q\) arm is delayed by \(T_b = T_s/2\) before its balance modulator.
  • Effect: the even and odd streams can no longer change at the same instant.
  • So only one of I or Q switches at a time \(\rightarrow\) maximum phase change is \(\pm 90^\circ\), never \(180^\circ\).
  • The envelope therefore never passes through zero, and band-limiting produces only shallow dips instead of nulls.
  • Hard-limiting or class-C amplification no longer regenerates the sidelobes, so OQPSK keeps its spectral occupancy in a real transmitter.
  • Phase transitions happen every \(T_b\) instead of every \(T_s\), i.e. twice as often but half as violent.
  • PSD, BER and bandwidth are identical to QPSK. The gain is purely in envelope behaviour.
OQPSK time offset: \(m_I(t)\) changes at even multiples of \(T\), \(m_Q(t)\) at odd multiples. Note the half-symbol offset. Rappaport Fig 5.30
Transmitter 2.5
  1. NRZ \(\rightarrow\) serial-to-parallel into \(m_I(t)\) and \(m_Q(t)\).
  2. Insert a \(T_b\) delay in the \(Q\) branch.
  3. \(m_I\) \(\times \cos 2\pi f_c t\), delayed \(m_Q\) \(\times \sin 2\pi f_c t\).
  4. Sum, then BPF \(\rightarrow\) OQPSK out.
Receiver 2.5
  1. Coherent, exactly the QPSK receiver: BPF, carrier recovery, two correlators, two decision circuits.
  2. The \(T_b\) stagger is removed by delaying the \(I\) decision (or advancing \(Q\)) before the multiplexer, so the dibits re-align.
  3. Symbol timing recovery is taken from the transitions, which now occur every \(T_b\).
\(\pi/4\)-QPSK: constellation (a) and constellation (b) are used on alternate symbols, giving the 8-state pattern below with all allowed transitions drawn. Rappaport Fig 5.31
\(\pi/4\)-QPSK, the compromise
  • Two QPSK constellations, offset from each other by \(\pi/4\), used on alternate symbols.
  • Signalling points therefore take 8 possible phase states, but only 4 are available in any one symbol.
  • Maximum phase change is limited to \(\pm 135^\circ\): worse than OQPSK's \(90^\circ\), much better than QPSK's \(180^\circ\).
  • Every symbol carries a phase transition (no \(0^\circ\) option), which makes clock recovery easy.
  • Usually sent differentially encoded as \(\pi/4\)-DQPSK.
  • Used in IS-136 (US digital cellular), PDC and PHS (Japan), TETRA.
Why \(\pi/4\)-QPSK is preferred over OQPSK 2
  1. It can be detected non-coherently. Because it is differentially encoded, a differential or discriminator detector works. OQPSK must be detected coherently, and the half-symbol offset makes differential detection impossible.
  2. Non-coherent detection \(\rightarrow\) no carrier recovery circuit \(\rightarrow\) far simpler, cheaper, faster-acquiring receiver.
  3. Better in multipath spread and fading, where a coherent receiver cannot hold a phase reference. This is the mobile channel exactly.
  4. Guaranteed transition every symbol \(\rightarrow\) reliable symbol timing recovery even on long runs of identical dibits.
  5. Cost accepted: envelope variation is larger than OQPSK's, so a mildly linear amplifier is still needed. verified/added

Which is suitable for GSM, and why 2
  • GMSK with \(BT = 0.3\). Three reasons, in order of weight:
    1. Constant envelope \(\rightarrow\) the handset can use a saturated class-C power amplifier \(\rightarrow\) battery life and cheap RF.
    2. Compact spectrum \(\rightarrow\) fits the 200 kHz GSM carrier with acceptable adjacent channel interference. MSK alone leaks too much.
    3. Detectable non-coherently by a simple FM discriminator, so the receiver stays cheap.
  • \(BT = 0.3\) is the chosen compromise: tight enough spectrum, ISI penalty still small enough to be equalized out.

column1: GMSK transmission and detection process, block diagram and constellation
column4:
What GMSK is
  • MSK preceded by a premodulation Gaussian low-pass filter.
  • The Gaussian filter has no zero crossings and no overshoot, so it smooths the rectangular data into a shape that suppresses the high-frequency content responsible for MSK's sidelobes.
  • Transfer function \(H(f) = e^{-\frac{\ln 2}{2}\left(f/B\right)^{2}}\), where \(B\) is the 3 dB bandwidth of the filter.
  • The filter is fully described by \(B\) and the symbol duration \(T\), so GMSK is named by its \(BT\) product. \(BT = \infty\) is plain MSK.
  • Smaller \(BT\): tighter spectrum, sidelobes fall away faster, but the pulse spreads over more symbols \(\rightarrow\) more ISI \(\rightarrow\) higher BER.
  • GSM: \(BT = 0.3\). CDPD and Mobitex also use GMSK.
  • Constellation: same 4 points as QPSK, but the trajectory between them follows the unit circle instead of cutting across it, which is the constant envelope drawn.
GMSK transmitter, FM route. SST Ch 4
GMSK transmitter, I-Q route. SST, Fig 3.2.17
GMSK detector, orthogonal coherent form. SST, Fig 3.2.18
Transmission process 3
  1. Data \(\rightarrow\) bipolar NRZ encoder \(\rightarrow\) \(\pm 1\) rectangular pulses.
  2. \(\rightarrow\) Gaussian LPF of bandwidth \(B\), which rounds every pulse edge.
  3. \(\rightarrow\) FM modulator set to modulation index exactly 0.5, driven by the carrier oscillator \(\cos\omega_c t\).
  4. Output is GMSK: constant amplitude, continuous smoothly varying phase.
  5. I-Q alternative (right-hand figure above): the filtered signal is integrated, split into in-phase and quadrature paths, each Gaussian-filtered and multiplied by \(\cos\omega_c t\) / \(\sin\omega_c t\), then subtracted. Advantage: the index stays at exactly 0.5 with no tuning or drift.
Detection process 3
  1. Coherent (orthogonal) detector, drawn left: GMSK splits into two arms.
  2. Each arm has a balance modulator fed by \(\cos\omega_c t\) or \(\sin\omega_c t\), then a Gaussian filter matched to the transmitter's.
  3. Each arm's decision device compares against its own threshold, giving \(I(t)\) and \(Q(t)\), which are recombined into the bit stream.
  4. Non-coherent alternative: a simple FM discriminator followed by an integrate-and-dump. Much cheaper, small BER penalty. This is what a GSM handset actually does.
Worked example: sizing the Gaussian filter verified/added (tutorial problem, never a PYQ)
PROBLEM SST tutorial · not from any paper
Find the 3-dB bandwidth for a Gaussian low pass filter used to produce 0.25 GMSK with a channel data rate of \(R_b = 270\) kbps. What is the 90 % power bandwidth in the RF channel?
Step 1: symbol duration
  • Binary GMSK, so one bit per symbol and \(T = 1/R_b = 1/270{,}000 = \mathbf{3.7\ \mu s}\).
Step 2: 3-dB bandwidth from the \(BT\) product
  • “0.25 GMSK” means \(BT = 0.25\), so \(B = 0.25/T = 0.25/3.7\ \mu\text{s} = \mathbf{67.57\ kHz}\).
Step 3: 90 % power RF bandwidth from the table
  • Read the occupied RF bandwidth table (§4.4 figure): row \(BT = 0.25\), column 90 % gives \(\mathbf{0.57 R_b}\).
  • RF BW \(= 0.57 \times 270{,}000 = \mathbf{153.9\ kHz}\).
Answer
  • 3-dB filter bandwidth \(B = \mathbf{67.57\ kHz}\).
  • 90 % power RF bandwidth \(= \mathbf{153.9\ kHz}\).
Notes on this problem
  • Real GSM uses \(BT = 0.3\) and \(R_b = 270.833\) kbps, not the rounded values here. Answer with whatever the paper prints.
  • The table is in units of \(R_b\), so always multiply the tabulated figure by the bit rate. Forgetting that is the standard slip.
  • Sanity check: 153.9 kHz sits inside GSM's 200 kHz carrier spacing, which is exactly the design intent.

column1: Why do we need M-ary QAM? Compare 16-QAM and 16-PSK using constellation diagrams
column4:
Why M-ary QAM is needed 2
  • Spectrum is licensed and finite, data demand is not. Binary schemes cap out near 1 bps/Hz.
  • M-ary raises \(\eta_B\) to \(\log_2 M\) bps/Hz without extra bandwidth.
  • But M-ary PSK alone fails at high \(M\): all points sit on one circle, so \(d_{\min}\) falls like \(\sin(\pi/M)\) and the power cost explodes.
  • QAM uses the radial dimension too. Spreading points over a 2-D grid gives a much larger \(d_{\min}\) for the same average power.
  • So M-ary QAM is the only practical way to reach 4, 6 or 8 bits per symbol on a band-limited channel.
16-PSK (left): 16 points on one circle, all at the same power, spacing \(22.5^\circ\). 16-QAM (right): 16 points on a \(4\times4\) grid, three different amplitudes. Same 4 bits per symbol either way. SST Ch 4
Parameter16-PSK16-QAM
Bits per symbol44
Bandwidthsamesame (identical symbol rate)
Constellation16 points, one circle\(4\times4\) grid, 3 amplitude levels
Envelopeconstantvaries
Amplifiernon-linear, efficientlinear, backed off
\(d_{\min}\) at equal peak powersmallerlarger
Power for the same \(d_{\min}\)1.6 dB more peak powerreference
Power at equal \(d_{\min}\) (average)4.19 dB more average power verified/addedreference
Noise immunityequal, if \(d_{\min}\) is equalisedequal, at less power
The number the examiner wants
  • At the same minimum Euclidean distance (the same noise immunity), 16-QAM needs 1.6 dB less peak power than 16-PSK.
  • Measured on average power instead, the gap is 4.19 dB verified/added.
  • Both figures describe the same fact: the grid packs 16 points more economically than the circle.
  • Careful: the lecture note's line “noise immunity is same” is only true when the two are compared at equal \(d_{\min}\). At equal transmit power 16-QAM is clearly better.
So why is 16-PSK used at all
  • Constant envelope \(\rightarrow\) the transmitter can saturate its amplifier.
  • 16-QAM's amplitude variation forces a linear amplifier with 6 to 8 dB of back-off, which gives back much of the 4.19 dB.
  • Rule of thumb: QAM on the downlink (base station has mains power), constant envelope on the uplink (handset does not).
  • Both need coherent detection and accurate gain control.
QAM modulator. SST, Fig 3.2.21
QAM modulator, walked through
  1. Binary stream at \(f_b\) enters a 2-bit serial-to-parallel converter (4-bit for 16-QAM), clocked at the symbol rate \(T_s\).
  2. Each half feeds a D/A converter that turns the bit group into a multi-level signal \(d_1(t)\) and \(d_2(t)\).
  3. \(d_1(t)\) multiplies \(\cos 2\pi f_c t\), \(d_2(t)\) multiplies \(\sin 2\pi f_c t\) (carrier through a \(\pi/2\) shifter).
  4. Summer adds the two \(\rightarrow\) a signal whose amplitude and phase both carry data.
  5. Demodulator is the QPSK receiver with A/D converters instead of 1-bit decision devices, plus a carrier recovery circuit (raise to 4th power, BPF at \(4f_c\), divide by 4).

column1: OFDM operation, block diagram of transmitter and receiver
column4:
The problem OFDM solves
  • Push the bit rate up on a single carrier and the symbol period \(T_s\) shrinks.
  • Once \(T_s\) approaches the channel's delay spread \(\sigma_\tau\), echoes of symbol \(n\) land on top of symbol \(n{+}1\) \(\rightarrow\) severe ISI and frequency-selective fading.
  • Fixing that in the time domain needs an equalizer with a great many taps, which is expensive and must adapt continuously.
  • OFDM's answer: do not make the symbol shorter, make it longer, and send many of them side by side.
The figure that answers “OFDM principle”. FDM (top) wastes spectrum on guard bands. OFDM (bottom) overlaps orthogonal subcarriers and needs none. AS Sir, OFDM notes
The principle 4
  • Split the high-rate stream into \(N\) parallel low-rate substreams.
  • Each substream modulates its own subcarrier, using QPSK or QAM.
  • Each subcarrier's symbol period becomes \(N T_s\), now much longer than the delay spread \(\rightarrow\) each subchannel sees flat fading, not selective.
  • Flat fading \(\rightarrow\) one complex multiply per subcarrier undoes the channel. The many-tap equalizer disappears.
  • Subcarrier spacing is set to \(\Delta f = 1/T\), which makes them orthogonal: each one's spectrum has a null exactly where every other one peaks.
  • So the spectra may overlap without interfering, and no guard bands are needed. Against FDM that is roughly a 50 % bandwidth saving.
  • The whole bank of \(N\) modulators is computed as one IFFT, and the bank of demodulators as one FFT. No oscillator bank, no filter bank.
Data is coded in the frequency domain, IFFT turns it into a time waveform, the channel acts, FFT recovers each subcarrier separately. AS Sir, OFDM notes
Draw exactly this for the 8-mark question. Transmitter on top, receiver below, channel and noise between them. AS Sir, OFDM notes
Transmitter chain 4
  1. Modulation / symbol mapping: bits \(\rightarrow\) QPSK or QAM symbols (after channel coding and interleaving).
  2. S/P: serial symbol stream split into \(N\) parallel subcarrier values, i.e. a frequency-domain block.
  3. IFFT: converts that block to \(N\) time-domain samples. This is the modulation.
  4. P/S: back to a serial sample stream.
  5. Insert CP: cyclic prefix prepended (see below).
  6. D/A \(\rightarrow\) up-convert to RF \(\rightarrow\) antenna.
Receiver chain 4
  1. Down-convert \(\rightarrow\) A/D.
  2. Synchronise: packet detection, then carrier frequency offset correction.
  3. Remove CP, discard the guard samples.
  4. S/P \(\rightarrow\) block of \(N\) time samples.
  5. FFT \(\rightarrow\) back to the frequency domain, one value per subcarrier.
  6. Equalize: divide each subcarrier by its estimated \(H[k]\), one tap each.
  7. P/S \(\rightarrow\) de-modulation / de-mapping \(\rightarrow\) deinterleave and decode \(\rightarrow\) data out.
Receiver is the transmitter read right to left. Say that and you have drawn half the answer.
Cyclic prefix, the detail that earns marks
  • Even with long symbols, the tail of one OFDM symbol still smears into the next.
  • A blank guard interval would work, but the hardware must transmit continuously and the exact delay spread is unknown.
  • Solution: copy the last \(T_g\) of the symbol and glue it on the front.
  • Two effects:
    • Any echo arriving within \(T_g\) falls inside the copied portion, so it corrupts only the prefix, which is thrown away \(\rightarrow\) ISI removed.
    • Linear convolution with the channel becomes circular convolution, so after the FFT each subcarrier is simply scaled: \(Y[k] = H[k]X[k]\) \(\rightarrow\) one-tap equalization.
  • Requirement: \(T_g >\) maximum delay spread. In 802.11, CP : data \(= 1:4\).
  • Side benefit: the packet still decodes even if detected a little late.
  • Cost: the CP is pure overhead, up to 20 to 25 % of throughput.
The tail of the symbol is copied to the front as an extension. AS Sir, OFDM notes
Two more practical details
  • Virtual (null) subcarriers at the band edges are left unused: edge bins are the most vulnerable to frequency offset, and the gap suppresses out-of-band radiation.
  • Pilot subcarriers carry known symbols so the receiver can track residual phase and estimate \(H[k]\).
  • 802.11a splits its 64 bins as 48 data \(+\) 4 pilot \(+\) 12 null verified/added. The lecture note's “48 of 64 occupied” counts only the data bins.
OFDM: advantages and disadvantages 4
PIN 1 82 Bh 4+4  \(\cdot\)  asked together with “draw the transmitting side”, so budget the time
Advantages
  • High spectral efficiency: overlapping orthogonal subcarriers, no guard bands, roughly twice FDM's.
  • Immune to ISI and frequency-selective fading: long symbols plus the CP.
  • Simple equalization: one complex multiply per subcarrier, no adaptive transversal filter.
  • Efficient to build: FFT/IFFT in DSP, cost grows as \(N\log N\), not \(N^2\).
  • Robust to narrowband interference: a jammer kills a few subcarriers, and coding \(+\) interleaving recovers them.
  • Flexible: power and modulation order can be set per subcarrier (adaptive bit loading); extends naturally to OFDMA and MIMO.
Disadvantages
  • High PAPR (peak-to-average power ratio): \(N\) subcarriers can add in phase, so the amplifier needs heavy back-off \(\rightarrow\) poor efficiency. The main drawback. It is why LTE uses SC-FDMA, not OFDMA, on the uplink.
  • Very sensitive to frequency offset and phase noise: any error destroys orthogonality \(\rightarrow\) inter-carrier interference (ICI).
  • Sensitive to Doppler: a fast-moving mobile changes the channel within one long symbol.
  • CP overhead wastes 20 to 25 % of both time and energy.
  • Tight synchronisation needed in both time and frequency.
Used in: DAB, DVB-T, 802.11a/g/n/ac, WiMAX, LTE downlink, 5G NR, ADSL.
