column1: Specifications of GSM; the radio subsystem and ARFCN
column4:
The radio plan
  • Two 25 MHz bands: 890–915 MHz reverse (MS to BS), 935–960 MHz forward (BS to MS).
  • Multiple access is FDD \(+\) TDMA over FDMA, with optional slow frequency hopping. See Ch 7 §7.3.
  • Each band is cut into 200 kHz carriers called ARFCNs, absolute radio frequency channel numbers.
  • One ARFCN names a forward and reverse pair 45 MHz apart, so an ARFCN is a duplex channel, not a single frequency.
  • \(25\ \text{MHz} / 200\ \text{kHz} = 125\) carriers, but a 100 kHz guard band is left at each edge, so only 124 duplex channels are usable, ARFCN 1 to 124.
  • Each 200 kHz carrier is time shared by 8 users using TDMA.
  • Physical channel \(=\) (ARFCN, time slot number). A logical channel is then mapped onto a physical channel, see §8.5.
  • DCS 1800 uses 1710–1785 / 1805–1880 MHz, three times the spectrum, giving 374 duplex channels.
Reproduce this table for a 5 specifications question. Rappaport Table 10.3, via SST Ch 8  \(\cdot\)  one printed value to know about: the table gives the voice coder at 13.4 kbps, while the RPE-LTP codec itself produces 260 bits per 20 ms \(=\) 13.0 kbps exactly (§8.7). Quote 13 kbps if you are asked for the codec rate. verified/added
Rates worth memorising
  • Modulation 0.3 GMSK, channel data rate 270.833 kbps per carrier.
  • Bandwidth efficiency \(= 270.833 / 200 = \mathbf{1.354}\) bps/Hz.
  • Per-user channel rate \(= 270.833 / 8 = \mathbf{33.854}\) kbps.
  • After all overhead, maximum user data rate 24.7 kbps.
  • Bit period 3.692 \(\mu\)s, time slot 576.9 \(\mu\)s, frame 4.615 ms.

column1: Draw and explain the GSM frame structure / channel structure / frame hierarchy
column4:
Draw the hierarchy top down and label the four durations. That is the whole answer to a 4 or 5 question. SST Ch 8
The five levels, bottom up
  1. Time slot \(=\) 156.25 bits \(=\) 576.92 \(\mu\)s. One burst.
  2. TDMA frame \(=\) 8 slots \(=\) 1250 bits \(=\) 4.615 ms \(\left(=120/26\ \text{ms}\right)\).
  3. Multiframe, two kinds:
    • 26-frame traffic multiframe \(=\) 120 ms. Carries TCH, SACCH, FACCH.
    • 51-frame control multiframe \(=\) 235.4 ms. Carries BCH and CCCH.
  4. Superframe \(=\) 51 traffic multiframes \(=\) 26 control multiframes \(=\) 1326 TDMA frames \(=\) 6.12 s.
  5. Hyperframe \(=\) 2048 superframes \(=\) 2 715 648 TDMA frames \(=\) 3 h 28 min 53.76 s.
Why a hyperframe at all: the ciphering algorithm and the hopping sequence are both driven by the frame number, so the frame number must not repeat for a long time.  \(\cdot\) Two multiframe sizes, one superframe: \(51 \times 26\) either way \(=\) 1326, which is exactly why 26 and 51 were chosen. verified/added  \(\cdot\) The SST slide prints the hyperframe as 3 h 28 min 52.76 s; \(2048 \times 6.12 = 12533.76\) s recomputes to 53.76 s. verified/added
One frame down to one normal burst. The 546.5 \(\mu\)s is the useful part, 577 \(\mu\)s is the whole slot including guard space. SST Ch 8
Inside a normal burst 3
  • 3 tail bits \((0,0,0)\) \(\rightarrow\) mark the start, let the equalizer settle.
  • 57 encrypted data bits.
  • 1 stealing flag \(\rightarrow\) says whether this half is user data or FACCH signalling.
  • 26 training bits \(\rightarrow\) a known sequence the receiver correlates against to build a channel model for the equalizer (Ch 5).
  • 1 stealing flag, 57 encrypted data bits, 3 tail bits.
  • 8.25 guard bits \(\rightarrow\) stop bursts from overlapping and give the power amplifier ramp-up and ramp-down time.
  • Total \(3+57+1+26+1+57+3 = \mathbf{148}\) useful \(+\ 8.25\) guard \(=\) 156.25 bits.
Five burst formats, all 156.25 bits. Rappaport Fig 10.9, via SST Ch 8
Why five formats
  • Normal burst \(\rightarrow\) TCH and most control channels.
  • FCCH burst \(\rightarrow\) 142 fixed bits, all zeros. Under GMSK an all-zero block becomes a pure tone, which is exactly what a mobile needs to pull its local oscillator onto the base station.
  • SCH burst \(\rightarrow\) a long 64-bit training sequence, because the mobile has no channel estimate yet.
  • RACH (access) burst \(\rightarrow\) 8 start bits and a 68.25-bit extended guard period. The mobile does not yet know its timing advance, so the burst is kept short to guarantee it cannot land on the next slot.
  • Dummy burst \(\rightarrow\) mixed bits, no information. Sent on unused slots of the BCH carrier so its power stays constant and neighbouring mobiles can measure it.
Traffic (speech) multiframe, 26 frames, 120 ms. SST Ch 8, Fig 11.7
Traffic multiframe 2
  • TCH data runs in consecutive frames, but frames 13 and 26 are not TCH.
  • Frame 13 carries SACCH.
  • Frame 26 carries idle bits for a full-rate TCH, and SACCH for a half-rate TCH.
  • The idle frame is what gives the mobile time to measure neighbouring cells for MAHO (Ch 2).
Control multiframe, 51 frames, 235 ms. (a) forward link on TS0, (b) reverse link on TS0. SST Ch 8, Fig 11.8
Control multiframe 2
  • Forward: F (FCCH) then S (SCH) repeat every 10 frames; between them sit B (BCCH) and C (PCH / AGCH) bursts, with one idle frame.
  • Reverse: all 51 frames are R, reverse RACH bursts. The uplink control channel is pure random access, so no structure is possible.
  • Both live in TS0 of the BCH ARFCN.
Frame efficiency, in one line 2
  • \(\eta_f = \left(1 - \dfrac{b_{OH}}{b_T}\right)\times 100\,\%\), with \(b_T = 8 \times 156.25 = 1250\) bits and \(b_{OH} = 8\,(6 + 8.25 + 26) = 322\) bits \(\rightarrow \eta_f = \mathbf{74.24\,\%}\).
  • It can never be 100 %: tail, training and guard bits are needed for the equalizer and for timing, and removing them breaks the link.
  • Full working, with the 74 Ma and 70 Bh statements, is in Ch 7 companion §3. Do not redo it here.

column1: Explain the working of all traffic and control channels used in GSM
column2: 45684+42+4
column4:
Draw this tree first, then write one line per leaf. SST Ch 8
Physical against logical
  • Physical channel \(=\) one ARFCN \(+\) one time slot number. Hardware.
  • Logical channel \(=\) a stream of a particular kind, mapped onto a physical channel. Meaning.
  • Many logical channels time-share the same physical channel over the multiframe.
Traffic channels (TCH) 2
  • Carry digitally encoded user speech or user data, both directions.
  • Full rate TCH/FS: a slot in every frame \(\rightarrow\) 22.8 kbps.
  • Half rate TCH/HS: a slot in every second frame \(\rightarrow\) 11.4 kbps, doubling the users per carrier.
  • Data variants: TCH/F9.6, F4.8, F2.4 and TCH/H4.8, H2.4.
1. Broadcast channels (BCH) forward only, on TS0 of the BCH ARFCN 4
  • BCCH, broadcast control channel.
    • Broadcasts cell and network identity, the list of channels in use, and the access parameters.
    • This is what a nearby mobile reads to identify a cell and lock on to it.
  • FCCH, frequency correction channel.
    • Occupies TS0 of the first frame, repeated every 10th frame of the control multiframe.
    • Lets each subscriber unit synchronise its local oscillator to the base station's exact frequency.
  • SCH, synchronisation channel.
    • Broadcast in TS0 immediately after an FCCH frame.
    • Identifies the serving base station and gives frame synchronisation; the base station also issues timing advance here.
2. Common control channels (CCCH) call establishment 4
  • Occupy TS0 of every control frame not used by the BCH or the idle frame.
  • PCH, paging channel, forward: notifies a specific mobile of an incoming call.
  • RACH, random access channel, reverse: the mobile acknowledges a page or originates a call. Contended, so collisions are possible and a random backoff is used.
  • AGCH, access grant channel, forward: the base station's answer to a RACH. Assigns a time slot, radio channel and dedicated control channel. AGCH is the last CCCH message before the mobile leaves the control channel.
3. Dedicated control channels (DCCH) both directions 4
  • Bidirectional, same format and function each way. May sit in any slot on any ARFCN except TS0 of the BCH ARFCN.
  • SDCCH, stand-alone dedicated control channel.
    • Signalling during idle periods and during call setup, before a TCH is allocated; released as soon as the TCH is assigned.
    • Carries authentication, ciphering setup, location update and SMS.
    • The intermediate channel that keeps mobile and base connected while resources are being allocated.
  • SACCH, slow associated control channel.
    • Always paired with a TCH or an SDCCH; occupies every 13th frame of the traffic multiframe.
    • Forward: power-level and timing-advance commands.
    • Reverse: received signal strength and quality reports for the serving cell and its neighbours \(\rightarrow\) this is what feeds MAHO.
  • FACCH, fast associated control channel.
    • Carries urgent signalling, above all handover commands.
    • Has no slots of its own: it steals a TCH burst, flagged by the two stealing bits in the normal burst.
    • Far faster than SACCH, at the cost of 20 ms of speech, which the speech decoder conceals.

column1: GSM frame structure; how traffic and control channels are used while making a call
column4:
Mobile-originated call setup, in order
  1. MS reads FCCH \(\rightarrow\) pulls its oscillator onto the base station.
  2. MS reads SCH \(\rightarrow\) frame synchronisation and base station identity.
  3. MS reads BCCH \(\rightarrow\) cell and network parameters. It is now camped on the correct BCH.
  4. To originate, MS sends a burst of RACH data on the same ARFCN it is locked to.
  5. Base station answers with an AGCH message on the CCCH, assigning an SDCCH.
Mobile-terminated differs in one step: the network first pages the mobile on the PCH, the mobile answers on the RACH, and everything from step 6 is identical. verified/added
Location updating, channel by channel: which logical channel carries each step when a mobile is switched on in a new area. Note how much of it rides on the SDCCH. SST Ch 8, Table 2.1
  1. MS, which is monitoring slot 0 of the BCH, reads its ARFCN and slot assignment from the AGCH and retunes to the SDCCH.
  2. Over the SDCCH the MS receives timing advance and power level commands. Only now can it send proper normal bursts.
  3. SDCCH carries authentication messages both ways. Meanwhile the PSTN connects the dialled party to the MSC, and the MSC switches the speech path to the serving base station.
  4. Base station commands the MS over the SDCCH to a new ARFCN and slot for the TCH.
  5. MS tunes to the TCH; speech flows both ways and the SDCCH is vacated.
What each stage costs, and why it is built this way
  • Steps 1–3 are listen only. The mobile transmits nothing until it has read the BCH, which is why a handset can be switched on inside a foreign network safely.
  • Step 4 is the only contended transmission in the whole sequence, so it uses the short RACH burst with its extended guard period (§8.4).
  • Step 7 exists because the mobile does not yet know its distance from the base station. Without timing advance its normal burst would overlap the next slot.
  • The SDCCH does all the work of call setup and is then thrown away. That is what “stand-alone dedicated” means: dedicated to one mobile, standing alone from any traffic channel.
  • Once on the TCH, further signalling has to steal bursts (FACCH) or wait for the 13th frame (SACCH), because there is no spare capacity left.

column1: Basic signal processing operations to convert speech to a radio signal and back
column4:
Draw the forward chain, then say the reverse is its mirror. The radio channel sits between modulation and demodulation. Rappaport Fig 10.11, via SST Ch 8
The chain, block by block
  1. Digitizing and source coding: RPE-LTP speech coder, 260 bits per 20 ms \(=\) 13 kbps.
  2. Channel coding: adds redundancy, 260 \(\rightarrow\) 456 bits \(=\) 22.8 kbps.
  3. Interleaving: the 456 bits are cut into eight 57-bit sub-blocks and spread over 8 consecutive TCH slots.
  4. Burst formatting: adds tail, training, stealing and guard bits \(\rightarrow\) the 156.25-bit burst of §8.4.
  5. Ciphering: A5 stream cipher, keystream XORed with the data bits.
  6. Modulation: 0.3 GMSK at 270.833 kbps.
  7. Radio channel, then demodulation, de-ciphering, burst formatting, de-interleaving, channel decoding, source decoding \(\rightarrow\) speech.
Speech coding 2
  • Coder is a RELP / RPE-LTP: residually excited linear predictor with a long term predictor. Full detail in Ch 6.
  • Output 260 bits per 20 ms frame. Half-rate codec runs at 6.5 kbps.
  • VAD \(=\) voice activity detector. Speech is active only about 40 % of the time, so DTX switches the transmitter off in the gaps.
  • DTX saves handset battery and cuts interference to other cells. Comfort noise is inserted at the far end so the line does not sound dead.
Channel coding 3
  • The 260 bits are sorted by how much they matter to speech quality:
    • 50 type Ia bits, most important \(\rightarrow\) 3 CRC parity bits added.
    • 132 type Ib bits, next.
    • 78 type II bits, least important \(\rightarrow\) no protection at all.
  • Types Ia and Ib \(+\) parity \(+\) 4 tail zeros \(= 189\) bits go through a rate 1/2, constraint length \(K=5\) convolutional encoder \(\rightarrow\) 378 bits.
  • \(378 + 78 = \mathbf{456}\) bits per 20 ms \(= \mathbf{22.8}\) kbps.
  • Unequal error protection: spending all the redundancy on the bits that would wreck the speech is what makes 13 kbps survive a fading channel.
260 bits in, 456 bits out. SST Ch 8
Interleaving, and why 8 slots
  • A deep fade wipes out a burst of adjacent bits, which no convolutional code handles well.
  • Spreading one speech frame over 8 bursts in 8 different frames turns one long error burst into eight short ones, one per code frame, which the decoder can fix.
  • Cost: about 40 ms of extra delay, which is why the specification table lists interleaving depth as a delay figure.
  • This is why a GSM call survives a moving car. The channel decorrelates between bursts, so eight bursts are eight independent looks at the same speech frame, i.e. time diversity (Ch 5).

column1: Frequency and channel specification of the IS-95 CDMA standard
column4:
IS-95, also called cdmaOne
  • A US standard built on Qualcomm's technology, the first commercial CDMA cellular system.
  • FDD, using two 1.25 MHz simplex channels 45 MHz apart.
    • Reverse (uplink) 824–849 MHz.
    • Forward (downlink) 869–894 MHz.
  • Chip rate 1.2288 Mcps, i.e. \(128 \times 9.6\) kbps.
  • Users in a cell and users in adjacent cells share the same radio channel, so the frequency reuse factor is \(N = 1\) and no frequency planning is needed. This is the single biggest planning advantage over GSM.
  • \(N=1\) is also what makes soft handoff possible: the mobile can be on the same carrier with two base stations at once (Ch 2).
  • Variable-rate vocoder: 9.6 / 4.8 / 2.4 / 1.2 kbps. Later EVRC gives 13 kbps quality at the 8 kbps rate.
The three code families 3
  • Walsh codes, 64 rows of a \(64\times64\) Hadamard matrix.
    • Forward link: one Walsh code per logical channel, so they separate channels.
    • Reverse link: 64-ary orthogonal modulation, so they separate groups of six symbols, not users. Learn this asymmetry, it is examinable.
  • Short PN codes, a quadrature pair of period \(2^{15}\) chips.
    • Applied on the I and Q arms after Walsh spreading.
    • Each cell or sector uses one of 512 phase offsets, so the short code identifies the sector.
  • Long PN code, period \(2^{42}-1\), generated from a 42-bit mask.
    • Forward: scrambles and encrypts the traffic, mask derived from the user's ESN.
    • Reverse: it is the channelising code \(-\) each mobile is separated by its own long-code phase.
Power control, because CDMA lives or dies by it 2
  • Open loop: the mobile measures the received pilot strength and sets its own transmit power inversely.
  • Closed loop: the base station measures each mobile and sends power control bits at 800 Hz, \(\pm 1\) dB per bit.
  • Without it the near-far problem (Ch 7 §7.6) destroys capacity.

column1: Draw and explain the forward CDMA (IS-95) channel; what is a channelization code?
column4:
Channelization code \(=\) Walsh code 2, built by the Hadamard recursion. Row \(n\) of the matrix is \(W_n\). Worked as a numerical in Ch 7 companion §4. SST Ch 8
Why Walsh codes work here
  • All 64 rows are mutually orthogonal: map \(0 \rightarrow -1\), \(1 \rightarrow +1\) and the term-by-term product of any two rows sums to 0.
  • So a receiver that correlates with \(W_n\) recovers channel \(n\) and sees exactly zero from the other 63, provided they arrive in step.
  • They stay in step on the forward link because one base station transmits them all. That is why the reverse link cannot use them for channelisation.
The four forward logical channels 4
  1. Pilot channel, \(W_0\).
    • Carries no baseband information at all: an all-zero stream, spread by \(W_0\) which is itself all zeros, so what goes out is the short PN pair itself at the sector's offset.
    • Transmitted continuously. Gives the mobile timing acquisition and a phase reference for coherent detection.
    • Its \(E_c/I_0\) is what the mobile measures to decide which sector is strongest, i.e. it drives handoff.
  2. Sync channel, \(W_{32}\).
    • 1.2 kbps of real baseband data, convolutionally coded and interleaved.
    • Carries the sync channel message: system time, long-code state, the sector's PN offset, and the paging channel rate (PRAT).
    • Uses the same PN offset as the pilot, so once the pilot is acquired the sync channel is readable at once.
  1. Paging channels, \(W_1\) to \(W_7\), up to seven.
    • 4.8 or 9.6 kbps, the rate announced by the sync message.
    • Overhead messages, pages, and traffic channel assignment during call setup.
    • A mobile monitors one paging channel, and ignores it once a traffic channel is up.
  1. Forward traffic channels, the remaining Walsh codes.
    • User voice and data at 1.2 / 2.4 / 4.8 / 9.6 kbps.
    • Structure is the paging channel plus one addition: multiplexed power control bits at 800 bps, punctured into the stream.
    • Scrambled by the long code with that user's ESN-derived mask.
Forward traffic channel, the block diagram to reproduce. Rate 1/2 \(K=9\) convolutional encoder \(\rightarrow\) symbol repetition to 19.2 ksps \(\rightarrow\) block interleaver \(\rightarrow\) long-code scrambling \(\rightarrow\) MUX with the 800 bps power control bits \(\rightarrow\) Walsh cover \(W_i\) \(\rightarrow\) I/Q short PN \(\rightarrow\) QPSK. SST Ch 8
The modulator, and how the channels combine 2
  • Every logical channel first passes a gain control block, which sets how much of the sector's power that channel gets.
    • Traffic channel gains change continuously, driven by forward power control.
    • Pilot gain is fixed and deliberately generous, typically 15 to 20 % of total power, because everything else depends on it. verified/added
  • After gain setting all channels are coherently added into one composite spread-spectrum signal.
  • The sum is split into I and Q, each spread by its short PN sequence, up-converted on quadrature carriers and added \(\rightarrow\) one QPSK passband signal.
  • One 1.25 MHz carrier therefore carries all 64 code channels of the sector at once.
Pilot channel 3. All zeros in, PN out. No encoder, no interleaver, nothing to decode. SSD, IS-95 channels
Sync channel 3. 1.2 kbps \(\rightarrow\) rate 1/2 \(\rightarrow\) 2.4 ksps \(\rightarrow\) repetition to 4.8 ksps \(\rightarrow\) interleave \(\rightarrow\) \(W_{32}\) \(\rightarrow\) I/Q PN. SSD, IS-95 channels
Paging channel. Same shape as the sync channel plus long-code scrambling through a decimator. SSD, IS-95 channels
Forward traffic channel. The paging channel plus the MUX that punctures in the 800 bps power control bits. SSD, IS-95 channels

column1: Draw the reverse CDMA (IS-95) channel
column4:
Two channels only, and no pilot
  • The reverse link supports access channels and traffic channels. That is all.
  • There is no reverse pilot in IS-95: it is impractical for every mobile to broadcast its own pilot sequence.
  • No pilot \(\rightarrow\) no phase reference \(\rightarrow\) the reverse link is non-coherent.
  • Non-coherent \(\rightarrow\) Walsh functions cannot channelise, because mobiles cannot be held chip-aligned with each other.
  • Instead each mobile is identified by its own long PN sequence, set by a mask derived from its ESN.
  • Walsh functions are still used, but for 64-ary orthogonal modulation: every six code symbols are sent as one of the 64 Walsh functions, and the base station decides which one by correlating against all 64.
  • Forward: Walsh separates channels. Reverse: Walsh represents symbols.
Reverse traffic and access channel generation. Rate 1/3 \(K=9\) encoder \(\rightarrow\) repetition to 28.8 ksps \(\rightarrow\) interleaver \(\rightarrow\) 64-ary orthogonal modulator, 307.2 kcps \(\rightarrow\) data burst randomizer \(\rightarrow\) long PN \(\rightarrow\) I/Q short PN with a half-chip delay on Q, giving OQPSK. SST Ch 8
1. Access channel
  • Used when the mobile has no traffic channel assigned: to register, originate calls, respond to pages and orders, and send overhead messages.
  • Baseband rate is fixed at 4.8 kbps.
  • Rate 1/3 convolutional encoder, not 1/2 as on the forward link. The reverse is the weaker of the two links (a handset transmits under a watt), so it is given more redundancy.
  • Symbol repetition doubles it to 28.8 ksps, then block interleaving, then the 64-ary orthogonal modulator.
2. Reverse traffic channel
  • Carries user voice, data and signalling at 1.2 / 2.4 / 4.8 / 9.6 kbps.
  • Structure is the access channel plus one block: the data burst randomizer.
  • The randomizer is the whole point. When the vocoder drops to a lower rate the repeated symbols are redundant, so the randomizer gates them off instead of transmitting them.
  • Result: the handset transmits only in pseudo-random bursts \(\rightarrow\) lower average power, longer battery life and less interference into every other user, which is capacity.
  • The forward link exploits the same voice activity differently: it lowers the energy per symbol rather than gating off, since the base station must keep the composite waveform continuous.
Access channel 2. Note the fixed 4.8 kbps input and the absence of a data burst randomizer. SSD, IS-95 channels
Reverse traffic channel 2. The one added block is the data burst randomizer. SSD, IS-95 channels

column1: Compare the system architecture of CDMA with LTE; mention the function of the entities
column4:
CDMA (IS-95 / cdma2000) architecture
  • MS \(\rightarrow\) BTS \(\rightarrow\) BSC \(\rightarrow\) MSC for voice, or PDSN for packet data.
  • BTS: radio, Walsh covering, power control commands.
  • BSC: radio resource control, soft handoff combining, and the vocoders.
  • MSC: circuit switching to the PSTN.
  • PCF \(+\) PDSN: the packet data path, bolted on later.
  • HLR / VLR / AuC: same roles as in GSM.
  • Hierarchical and circuit-first: voice and data ride separate cores.
LTE (EPS) architecture
  • UE \(\rightarrow\) eNodeB \(\rightarrow\) EPC (MME, S-GW, P-GW) \(\rightarrow\) external IP networks.
  • eNodeB: radio plus all the radio resource control that a BSC used to do. There is no controller node. eNodeBs talk to each other directly over X2.
  • MME, control plane only: attach, authentication, bearer setup, mobility and paging.
  • S-GW: user-plane anchor, forwards packets during inter-eNodeB handover.
  • P-GW: IP anchor to the outside world, allocates the IP address, enforces policy, does charging.
  • HSS: subscriber database, HLR \(+\) AuC in one.
  • PCRF: policy and charging rules.
  • Flat and all-IP: two nodes from handset to internet, and no circuit domain at all.
The three differences to write down 3
  • Topology: CDMA is BTS–BSC–MSC, three tiers. LTE is eNodeB–EPC, two tiers. The BSC's job moved into the base station, which cuts handover latency.
  • Bearer: CDMA is circuit-switched voice with packet data added later. LTE is all-IP, packet only; voice comes back as VoLTE over IMS.
  • Air interface: 1.25 MHz DS-CDMA against OFDMA down, SC-FDMA up, with MIMO, on a scalable 1.4 to 20 MHz carrier. Peak rate rises from about 3 Mbps to 100 Mbps and beyond.

column1: AMPS, CT2, DECT, PHS, PACS, IS-54 / IS-136, IS-94, IS-95: the standards named in the syllabus
column4:
First generation, analog cellular
  • All FM voice with FSK signalling, FDMA/FDD, one carrier per user for the whole call.
  • AMPS, the Americas: 824–849 / 869–894 MHz, 30 kHz channels, 832 channels.
  • TACS / ETACS, UK and Europe: 25 kHz channels, up to 1240 channels.
  • NMT-450 / NMT-900, the Nordic countries, 25 and 12.5 kHz.
  • C-450 Germany, RTMS Italy, Radiocom 2000 France, NTT and JTACS/NTACS Japan.
  • Every country built its own, which is exactly the fragmentation GSM was created to end.
Rappaport Table 10.10
Digital cordless standards. Rappaport Table 10.11
Second generation digital cellular. Rappaport Table 10.12
Cordless and PCS, the short-range family
  • CT2, Europe and Canada, 864–868 MHz, TDD, 100 kHz carriers, one channel per carrier, 72 kbps GFSK, ADPCM speech.
  • DECT, Europe, 1880–1900 MHz, TDD, 1728 kHz carriers with 12 channels each, 1152 kbps GFSK. The one that survived, as the office and home cordless phone.
  • PHS, Japan, 1895–1918 MHz, TDD, 300 kHz, 4 channels per carrier, 384 kbps \(\pi/4\)-DQPSK.
  • PACS, USA, FDD or TDD, 300 kHz, 8 or 4 channels per carrier, 384 kbps \(\pi/4\)-QPSK. Designed for licensed PCS microcells.
  • IS-94 is the odd one out: it is not cordless but the standard for AMPS-based private and in-building microcell systems, i.e. cellular hardware reused as a premises system. verified/added
  • All of them are TDD, low power and short range, which is what separates a cordless standard from a cellular one.
Second generation, digital cellular
  • GSM (1990): TDMA/FDMA/FDD, 200 kHz, GMSK \(BT = 0.3\), 270.833 kbps, RPE-LTP at 13 kbps, 1.35 bps/Hz.
  • IS-54, later IS-136, also called USDC or D-AMPS (1991): 30 kHz channels, deliberately the same as AMPS so the two could share a band, 3 users per carrier, \(\pi/4\)-DQPSK at 48.6 kbps, VSELP 7.95 kbps.
  • PDC, Japan (1993): 25 kHz, \(\pi/4\)-DQPSK at 42 kbps, VSELP 6.7 kbps, 1.68 bps/Hz, the most spectrally efficient of the three.
  • IS-95 (1993): the CDMA outlier, 1.25 MHz carriers, \(N=1\). §8.8.
  • Three of the four are TDMA. CDMA was the minority choice in 2G and the majority choice in 3G.

column1: Write short notes on WiMAX / LTE
column4:
WiMAX 4
  • WiMAX \(=\) worldwide interoperability for microwave access, the trade name for IEEE 802.16. A WMAN, one step above WiFi's WLAN.
  • Two versions worth naming:
    • 802.16d (2004), fixed WiMAX, OFDM.
    • 802.16e (2005), mobile WiMAX, scalable OFDMA, supports handover at vehicular speed.
  • Bands: 2–11 GHz for NLOS, 10–66 GHz for LOS backhaul. Scalable channel bandwidth 1.25 to 20 MHz.
  • Throughput about 75 Mbps fixed, 15 Mbps mobile; range 5–8 km NLOS, up to 50 km LOS.
  • The MAC is the real difference from WiFi: connection-oriented and scheduled by the base station, not contended. Every subscriber gets a grant, so QoS classes (UGS, rtPS, nrtPS, best effort) are enforceable.
  • Topologies: point-to-multipoint, and mesh.
  • Uses: last-mile broadband where cable is uneconomic, backhaul for WiFi hotspots and cell sites, rural and disaster-recovery connectivity.
  • (-): needs licensed spectrum, expensive base stations, and it lost the 4G market to LTE because operators already owned 3GPP cores.
LTE 3
  • LTE \(=\) long term evolution, 3GPP Release 8 (2008). The 4G standard that won.
  • OFDMA on the downlink, SC-FDMA on the uplink. SC-FDMA is chosen purely for its low PAPR, which is what a battery-powered handset amplifier needs (Ch 4 §4.6).
  • MIMO up to \(4\times4\), scalable bandwidth 1.4 / 3 / 5 / 10 / 15 / 20 MHz, both FDD and TDD.
  • Release 8 peaks at about 300 Mbps down, 75 Mbps up.
  • Flat all-IP architecture, §8.11. No circuit-switched domain: voice is VoLTE over IMS.
  • LTE-Advanced (Rel 10) adds carrier aggregation, \(8\times8\) MIMO, relay nodes and CoMP, reaching 1 Gbps.
The other names on the syllabus 2
  • UMTS: 3GPP's 3G. W-CDMA, 5 MHz carriers, 3.84 Mcps. Radio network is NodeB \(+\) RNC, reusing the GSM/GPRS core. HSPA later takes it to 14.4 Mbps.
  • CDMA-EVDO: cdma2000 1xEV-DO, “evolution, data optimised”. A separate 1.25 MHz data-only carrier with a time-multiplexed forward link and rate adaptation. Rev 0 gives 2.4 Mbps, Rev A 3.1 Mbps down / 1.8 Mbps up.
  • UMB: ultra mobile broadband, 3GPP2's OFDMA answer to LTE. Abandoned in 2008 when Qualcomm stopped development and the CDMA operators moved to LTE. Worth one honest line: it is on the syllabus but was never deployed. verified/added
Recent trends 2
  • 5G NR: sub-6 GHz plus mmWave, massive MIMO and beamforming, network slicing, three service classes eMBB / URLLC / mMTC.
  • IoT: NB-IoT and LTE-M, narrowband, low power, huge device counts.
  • D2D device-to-device, C-RAN centralised baseband, edge computing.
  • Cross-refer Ch 1 §1.4, which answers the “trends beyond 3G” question in full. Do not repeat it here.

column1: Describe regulatory issues in wireless communication: spectrum allocation, pricing, licensing, tariffs, interconnection
column4:
Why regulation exists at all 2
  • Radio spectrum is a finite, non-storable, shared natural resource.
  • Interference is non-excludable: two users on the same frequency, in the same place, at the same time both fail. Neither can protect itself.
  • So a government must decide who may use which band, where, and on what terms. That is spectrum management.
  • Significance of spectrum management 2:
    • Interference-free coexistence of services.
    • Efficient use of a scarce resource, and no hoarding.
    • International harmonisation \(\rightarrow\) roaming, economies of scale in handsets.
    • Protected bands for aviation, defence, emergency and scientific use.
    • Predictable rules \(\rightarrow\) operators will invest.
1. Spectrum allocation
  • ITU-R divides the world into three Regions and allocates bands to services at the World Radiocommunication Conference.
  • The national regulator then assigns those bands to operators: NTA in Nepal, FCC in the USA, CEPT/ETSI in Europe.
  • Assignment methods: administrative (a “beauty contest” on merit), auction, lottery, first-come first-served, or left unlicensed as a commons (the ISM bands WiFi and Bluetooth live in).
2. Spectrum pricing
  • Charges an operator for holding spectrum: an annual royalty per MHz per head of population, or the one-off auction price.
  • Aim: make idle spectrum expensive, so it moves to whoever will use it best.
  • Risk: overpricing is passed straight to the subscriber as tariff, and slows rural rollout. The regulator has to balance revenue against coverage.
3. Licensing
  • Decides who may operate, over what area, for how long, and on renewal terms.
  • Attaches obligations: coverage targets, quality of service, rural rollout, lawful interception.
  • Spectrum caps stop one operator cornering the band and keep the market competitive.
  • Type approval: only equipment that meets emission limits may be connected.
  • Technology-neutral licences let an operator refarm a 2G band for LTE without a new licence.
4. Tariff regulation
  • Regulator approves tariffs, and classifies them as fixed, maximum, or non-regulated.
  • Price caps and floors protect subscribers from a dominant operator and rivals from predatory pricing.
  • Tariffs are usually deregulated as competition arrives.
5. Interconnection
  • Every licensee must be able to terminate calls on every other network, otherwise the first operator to scale wins by default.
  • Regulator sets cost-oriented interconnection charges, the points of interconnection, and number portability.
  • It also settles interconnection disputes, which is why dispute resolution appears in the list of functions below.
Functions of the regulator 4 the list 80 Ch and 79 Ch want
  1. Inspection and investigation of the affairs of telecom operators and internet service providers.
  2. Settle disputes between licensees, or between a licensee and a customer, relating to telecommunications service.
  3. Determine the quality and standard of the machinery, equipment and facilities used, and of the service itself.
  4. Licensing of telecom operators and internet service providers.
  5. Approval of tariffs: fixed tariffs, maximum tariffs and non-regulated tariffs.
SST Ch 8, the NTA regulatory approach  \(\cdot\)  write these five and the 4 marks are secure. Add spectrum allocation and monitoring as a sixth if the question says “spectrum management”.
Nepal, if a local example is wanted verified/added
  • NTA \(=\) Nepal Telecommunications Authority, constituted under the Telecommunications Act 2053.
  • Licence categories it issues include basic telephony, cellular mobile, internet service, VSAT and rural VSAT, network service providers, international trunk telephone and rural ISP.
  • Naming NTA and the Act is enough for a Nepali paper. Do not attempt licence counts, they change every year.
Answer skeleton 5
  1. One line: spectrum is finite and shared, so it must be regulated. 1
  2. Name the five heads: allocation, pricing, licensing, tariff, interconnection. 1
  3. Two sentences on each head. 2.5
  4. Close with ITU-R above and the national regulator (NTA) below. 0.5
